exercises.instructions: Convert an array of `[key, value]` pairs into a single object. If a key appears more than once, the last value wins.
hints: Start with an empty object. For each pair, use the first element as the key and the second as the value. Assign `acc[pair[0]] = pair[1]`.
Each pair is a two-element array. Access `pair[0]` for the key and `pair[1]` for the value. Return the accumulator after each assignment.

exercises.title: every: Basics
exercises.description: Use every to check if all elements in an array pass a test.
exercises.instructions:
The `.every()` method tests whether all elements in an array pass the callback's test. It returns `true` only if the callback returns `true` for every element. If any element fails, it returns `false` immediately. An empty array returns `true` (vacuous truth).

Write a function that checks if every number in an array is positive using `.every()` (see `@param`/`@returns` in the starter code).

Example: `allPositive([1, 2, 3])` returns `true`
Example: `allPositive([1, -2, 3])` returns `false`
Example: `allPositive([])` returns `true`
hints: The `.every()` method returns `true` only when the callback returns `true` for all elements. Check whether each number is greater than zero.
Call `nums.every(function(n) { return n > 0; })` and return the result. It stops early on the first `false`.

exercises.title: some: Basics
exercises.description: Use some to check if at least one element passes a test.
exercises.instructions: Check if any number in the array is negative. Return `true` if at least one number is less than 0, otherwise `false`. Use `.some()`.
hints: The `.some()` method returns `true` as soon as the callback returns `true` for any element. Check if each number is less than zero.
Call `nums.some(function(n) { return n < 0; })`. It returns `true` on the first negative number found.

exercises.title: every and some: Combined
exercises.description: Use both every and some to validate an array against multiple criteria.
exercises.instructions: Validate an array of scores. Return `true` only if every score is between 0 and 100 (inclusive) AND at least one score is 90 or above.
hints: Use `.every()` to check that all scores are within 0-100. Use `.some()` to check that at least one score is 90 or above. Both conditions must be true.
Combine the results with `&&`: `allValid && hasHigh`. Use `s >= 0 && s <= 100` for the every check and `s >= 90` for the some check.

exercises.title: every and some: Validation
exercises.description: Use every and some to build a validation summary object.
exercises.instructions: Analyze an array of numbers against a min-max range. Return an object with three boolean properties: `allInRange` (every number is between min and max inclusive), `hasMin` (at least one number equals min), and `hasMax` (at least one number equals max).
hints: Build a return object with three properties. Use `.every()` for the range check and `.some()` for each boundary check.

Build a return object with three keys. Use `.every()` for the range check (two conditions joined with `&&`) and `.some()` for each boundary equality check. Each callback is a simple one-condition test.

exercises.title: sort: Numbers
exercises.description: Use sort with a compare function to sort numbers in ascending order.
exercises.instructions:
The `.sort()` method sorts an array in place. Without a compare function, it converts elements to strings and sorts lexicographically (which gives wrong results for numbers). To sort numbers correctly, pass a compare function: `function(a, b) { return a - b; }` for ascending order.

Write a function that returns a new array of numbers sorted in ascending order. Do not mutate the original array — use `.slice()` first (see `@param`/`@returns` in the starter code).

Example: `sortAscending([3, 1, 2])` returns `[1, 2, 3]`
Example: `sortAscending([])` returns `[]`
hints: Use `.slice()` to create a copy before sorting. The compare function `function(a, b) { return a - b; }` sorts numbers ascending — negative means a comes first, positive means b comes first.
Chain the calls: `nums.slice().sort(function(a, b) { return a - b; })`. Slice creates the copy, sort reorders it, and you return the result.

exercises.title: sort: Strings
exercises.description: Use sort with a compare function for case-insensitive alphabetical ordering.
exercises.instructions: Sort an array of strings alphabetically, ignoring case. Do not mutate the original array. Preserve the original casing in the output.
hints: Convert both strings to lowercase inside the compare function before comparing. Use `<` and `>` operators to determine order. Return -1, 0, or 1.
In the compare function, use `a.toLowerCase()` and `b.toLowerCase()`. Return `-1` if a comes first, `1` if b comes first, `0` if equal.

exercises.title: sort: Objects
exercises.description: Use sort with a compare function to order objects by a numeric property.
exercises.instructions: Sort an array of person objects by their `age` property in ascending order. Do not mutate the original array.
hints: Use the subtraction trick in the compare function: `a.age - b.age`. Negative means a comes first, positive means b comes first.
Chain `.slice().sort(function(a, b) { return a.age - b.age; })` to create a sorted copy without modifying the original.

exercises.title: sort: Multi-Key
exercises.description: Use sort with a compare function that handles multiple sort criteria.
exercises.instructions: Sort an array of student objects by `grade` descending (highest first), then by `name` ascending (alphabetical) as a tiebreaker. Do not mutate the original array.
hints: In the compare function, first check if grades differ — if so, sort by grade descending (`b.grade - a.grade`). Only when grades are equal, compare names alphabetically.
Use `if (a.grade !== b.grade) return b.grade - a.grade` for the primary sort. For the tiebreaker, use string comparison: `if (a.name < b.name) return -1; if (a.name > b.name) return 1; return 0`.

exercises.title: Method Chaining: Filter and Map
exercises.description: Chain filter and map to select and transform elements in one expression.
exercises.instructions:
Method chaining lets you call multiple array methods back-to-back. Each method returns a new array, which the next method operates on: `arr.filter(...).map(...)`. This avoids intermediate variables and reads like a pipeline.

Write a function that filters an array to keep only even numbers, then doubles each one — all in a single chained expression (see `@param`/`@returns` in the starter code).

Example: `getEvenDoubles([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6])` returns `[4, 8, 12]`
Example: `getEvenDoubles([1, 3, 5])` returns `[]`
hints: Chain two calls: first `.filter()` to keep evens (check `n % 2 === 0`), then `.map()` to double each remaining number.
Call `.filter()` first to keep even numbers, then chain `.map()` on the result to double each value. The output of the first method feeds directly as input to the second.

exercises.title: Method Chaining: Map, Filter, and Reduce
exercises.description: Chain map, filter, and reduce to transform, select, and accumulate in one pipeline.
exercises.instructions: Calculate the sum of squares of only the positive numbers. Chain `.filter()` to keep positives, `.map()` to square them, and `.reduce()` to sum the results.
hints: Build a three-step pipeline: filter positives (`n > 0`), map each to its square (`n * n`), then reduce the squares to a sum.
Chain: `.filter(function(n) { return n > 0; }).map(function(n) { return n * n; }).reduce(function(acc, n) { return acc + n; }, 0)`.

exercises.title: Method Chaining: Sort and Slice
exercises.description: Chain sort and slice to extract the top N values from an array.
exercises.instructions: Return the top `n` largest numbers from the array, sorted from highest to lowest. Do not mutate the original array.
hints: Use `.slice()` to copy, `.sort()` with a descending comparator (`b - a`), then `.slice(0, n)` to take the first n elements.
Chain: `nums.slice().sort(function(a, b) { return b - a; }).slice(0, n)`. The first slice copies, sort reorders, second slice trims.

exercises.title: Method Chaining: Chain with Find
exercises.description: Chain filter and sort to locate the cheapest in-stock product.
exercises.instructions: Find the name of the cheapest in-stock product. Filter to products where `inStock` is `true`, sort by `price` ascending, and return the `name` of the first result. Return `null` if no products are in stock.
hints: Filter to in-stock products, sort by price ascending, then check if any remain. If so, return the first product's name; otherwise return null.
Chain `.filter(function(p) { return p.inStock; }).sort(function(a, b) { return a.price - b.price; })`, then check the result length before accessing `[0].name`.

exercises.title: Method Chaining: Complex Pipeline
exercises.description: Build a multi-step pipeline to process transaction data.
exercises.instructions: Process an array of transactions. Filter to only `"completed"` transactions, extract their amounts, keep only positive amounts, and sum them.
hints: Build a four-step chain: filter by status, map to extract amounts, filter to keep positives, reduce to sum. Each step feeds into the next.
Chain `.filter(status === "completed").map(get amount).filter(amount > 0).reduce(sum, 0)`. Each method returns a new array for the next to work with.

exercises.title: Callback Methods: Top Words
exercises.description: Combine multiple callback methods to find the most frequent words in a text.
exercises.instructions: Find the top `n` most frequent words in a text string. Split the text into lowercase words, count occurrences, and return the top n as an array of `{word, count}` objects sorted by count descending. Ignore empty strings from splitting.
hints: Split and lowercase the text, filter empty strings, reduce to a counts object, convert keys to {word, count} objects with map, sort by count descending, then slice.
Pipeline: `text.toLowerCase().split(" ")` → `.filter()` → `.reduce()` to tally → `Object.keys(counts).map()` → `.sort()` → `.slice(0, n)`.

exercises.title: Callback Methods: Grade Analyzer
exercises.description: Combine callback methods to produce a statistical summary of student grades.
exercises.instructions: Analyze an array of student objects. Return an object with: `average` (mean grade), `highest` (max grade), `lowest` (min grade), `passing` (count with grade >= 60), and `failing` (count with grade < 60).
hints: Use `.map()` to extract grades, `.reduce()` for the sum, `.sort()` to find highest and lowest, and `.filter()` to count passing. Combine all into a return object.
Extract grades first: `students.map(function(s) { return s.grade; })`. Then build each stat: sum/length for average, sorted ends for high/low, filter for passing count.

exercises.title: Callback Methods: Inventory Manager
exercises.description: Combine callback methods to summarize product inventory data.
exercises.instructions: Summarize an array of products. Return an object with: `totalValue` (sum of price * quantity for all products), `inStock` (count where quantity > 0), `outOfStock` (count where quantity === 0), and `mostExpensive` (name of the product with the highest price).
hints: Use `.reduce()` for totalValue (price * quantity sum), `.filter()` for inStock count, and `.sort()` by price descending to find the most expensive.
Build each stat separately: `products.reduce(...)` for total, `products.filter(...).length` for inStock, `products.slice().sort(...)[0].name` for mostExpensive.

exercises.title: Callback Methods: Student Roster
exercises.description: Combine callback methods to group students and sort each group alphabetically.
exercises.instructions: Group students by their `gradeLevel` property. Return an object where each key is a grade level and each value is a sorted array of student names in that level.
hints: Use `.reduce()` to group students by gradeLevel, pushing names into arrays. Then use `Object.keys().forEach()` to sort each group's array alphabetically.
In the reduce callback, check if the group exists, create it if not, and push the name. After building the groups, iterate keys and call `.sort()` on each array.

exercises.title: Callback Methods: Data Pipeline
exercises.description: Build a comprehensive data pipeline combining all major callback methods.
exercises.instructions: Process employee records. Filter to only active employees, then return an object with: `departments` (array of unique department names, sorted alphabetically), `totalSalary` (sum of active salaries), `count` (number of active employees), and `averageSalary` (totalSalary / count, or 0 if no active employees).
hints: Filter active records first. Then use `.map()` to extract departments, filter for unique values, and sort. Use `.reduce()` for totalSalary. Build the return object from these pieces.

After filtering active records, extract departments with `.map()`, remove duplicates by checking if each element's `.indexOf()` matches its current index, then `.sort()`. Use `.reduce()` to sum salaries. Guard against dividing by zero when computing the average.

exercises.title: Closures: Counter
exercises.description: Create a closure that maintains a private count with increment, decrement, and getCount methods.
exercises.instructions:
A closure is a function that "remembers" variables from its outer scope even after the outer function has returned. This lets you create private state that can only be accessed through the returned functions.

Write a function that returns an object with three methods: `increment()` adds 1 to a private counter, `decrement()` subtracts 1, and `getCount()` returns the current value. The counter starts at 0 (see `@param`/`@returns` in the starter code).

Example: `const c = createCounter(); c.increment(); c.increment(); c.getCount()` returns `2`
Example: `const c = createCounter(); c.decrement(); c.getCount()` returns `-1`
Example: `createCounter().getCount()` returns `0`
hints: Declare a variable inside the outer function to hold the count. Return an object whose methods read and modify that variable. Each call to the outer function creates a new, independent scope.
Use `var count = 0;` inside `createCounter`. Return an object with `increment`, `decrement`, and `getCount` methods that use `count += 1`, `count -= 1`, and `return count` respectively.

exercises.title: Closures: Private State
exercises.description: Create a closure that encapsulates a private balance with deposit, withdraw, and getBalance methods.
hints: Use the same pattern as a counter closure, but add validation. Deposits should only work for positive amounts. Withdrawals should only work when the amount is positive and does not exceed the balance.
In `deposit`, check `if (amount > 0)` before adding. In `withdraw`, check `if (amount > 0 && amount <= balance)` before subtracting. Return the balance from `getBalance`.
exercises.instructions: Create a closure that encapsulates a private balance with deposit, withdraw, and getBalance methods.

exercises.title: Closures: Function Factory
exercises.description: Create a function that accepts a factor and returns a new function that multiplies any number by that factor.
hints: The outer function receives the `factor` and returns a new function. The inner function receives a number and uses the closed-over `factor` to compute the result.
Return `function(num) { return num * factor; }` from inside `createMultiplier`. The returned function remembers `factor` from its outer scope.
exercises.instructions: Create a function that accepts a factor and returns a new function that multiplies any number by that factor.

exercises.title: Closures: Accumulator
exercises.description: Create a closure that keeps a running total — each call adds to the total and returns the new sum.
hints: Store the initial value in a variable. Return a function that adds its argument to that variable and returns the updated total. Each accumulator instance should be independent.

Declare a variable initialized to the starting value. Return an inner function that adds its argument to that variable and returns the updated total. The outer variable persists between calls via closure.
exercises.instructions: Create a closure that keeps a running total — each call adds to the total and returns the new sum.

exercises.title: Higher-Order Functions: Accept Callback
exercises.description: Write a function that takes an array and a callback, applies the callback to each element, and returns a new array.
exercises.instructions:
A higher-order function is a function that either accepts a function as an argument, returns a function, or both. The `.map()`, `.filter()`, and `.reduce()` methods you already know are all higher-order functions built into arrays.

Write your own version of `.map()` from scratch. It should accept an array and a callback function, apply the callback to each element, and return a new array of the results (see `@param`/`@returns` in the starter code).

Example: `applyToEach([1, 2, 3], function(n) { return n * 2; })` returns `[2, 4, 6]`
Example: `applyToEach(["a", "b"], function(s) { return s + "!"; })` returns `["a!", "b!"]`
Example: `applyToEach([], function(n) { return n; })` returns `[]`
hints: Create an empty result array. Use a `for` loop to iterate through the input array, calling the callback on each element and pushing the return value into the result.
Create an empty array for results. Loop through the input array, calling the callback on each element and pushing the return value into your results array. Return the completed array at the end.

exercises.title: Higher-Order Functions: Return Function
exercises.description: Write a function that accepts a greeting string and returns a new function that greets any name with that greeting.
hints: Return a function from inside `createGreeter`. The inner function takes a `name` parameter and concatenates the greeting, a comma-space, the name, and an exclamation mark.
Return `function(name) { return greeting + ", " + name + "!"; }`. The returned function closes over the `greeting` variable from the outer scope.
exercises.instructions: Write a function that accepts a greeting string and returns a new function that greets any name with that greeting.

exercises.title: Higher-Order Functions: Compose
exercises.description: Write a function that accepts two single-argument functions and returns a new function applying them right-to-left.
hints: Compose means "apply g first, then apply f to the result." Return a new function that calls `g(x)` and passes that result to `f`.
Return `function(x) { return f(g(x)); }`. The key is the right-to-left order: `g` runs first, then `f` wraps the result.
exercises.instructions: Write a function that accepts two single-argument functions and returns a new function applying them right-to-left.

exercises.title: Higher-Order Functions: Pipe
exercises.description: Write a function that accepts two single-argument functions and returns a new function applying them left-to-right.
hints: Pipe is the reverse of compose — apply `f` first, then pass the result to `g`. Return a new function that chains them left-to-right.
Return `function(x) { return g(f(x)); }`. Notice this is the mirror of compose: `f` runs first, then `g` wraps the result.
exercises.instructions: Write a function that accepts two single-argument functions and returns a new function applying them left-to-right.

exercises.title: Function Composition: Compose N
exercises.description: Write a function that accepts any number of single-argument functions and returns a new function applying them right-to-left.
exercises.instructions:
You have already written `compose` for two functions. Now generalize it to accept any number of functions. Given `composeAll(f, g, h)`, the result should apply them right-to-left: `f(g(h(x)))`.

You can use `.reduceRight()` to fold an array of functions from right to left, passing the accumulated result through each one (see `@param`/`@returns` in the starter code).

Example: `composeAll(double, addOne, square)(3)` applies square(3)=9, addOne(9)=10, double(10)=20
Example: `composeAll(addOne)(5)` returns `6`
Example: `composeAll(double, double)(3)` returns `12`
hints: Collect the arguments into an array. Return a function that uses `.reduceRight()` to apply each function from right-to-left, starting with the input value as the initial accumulator.
Return `function(x) { return fns.reduceRight(function(acc, fn) { return fn(acc); }, x); }`. The `x` serves as the initial value, and each function transforms the accumulator.

exercises.title: Function Composition: Pipe N
exercises.description: Write a function that accepts any number of single-argument functions and returns a new function applying them left-to-right.
hints: This is the mirror of `composeAll`. Use `.reduce()` instead of `.reduceRight()` to apply functions left-to-right.
Return `function(x) { return fns.reduce(function(acc, fn) { return fn(acc); }, x); }`. The only difference from `composeAll` is `.reduce()` vs `.reduceRight()`.
exercises.instructions: Write a function that accepts any number of single-argument functions and returns a new function applying them left-to-right.

exercises.title: Function Composition: Predicate Combiner
exercises.description: Write a function that accepts an array of predicate functions and returns a new predicate that returns true only if all predicates pass.
hints: Return a function that tests the value against every predicate. You can use `.every()` to check that all predicates return `true` for the given value.
Return `function(value) { return predicates.every(function(pred) { return pred(value); }); }`. The `.every()` method short-circuits on the first `false`.
exercises.instructions: Write a function that accepts an array of predicate functions and returns a new predicate that returns true only if all predicates pass.

exercises.title: Currying: Two Arguments
exercises.description: Write a function that accepts a two-argument function and returns a curried version.
exercises.instructions:
Currying transforms a function that takes multiple arguments into a sequence of functions that each take one argument. Instead of calling `add(1, 2)`, a curried version is called as `curriedAdd(1)(2)`.

Write a function that takes any two-argument function and returns a curried version: `curry2(fn)(a)(b)` should equal `fn(a, b)` (see `@param`/`@returns` in the starter code).

Example: `curry2(function(a, b) { return a + b; })(1)(2)` returns `3`
Example: `var add1 = curry2(function(a, b) { return a + b; })(1); add1(5)` returns `6`
Example: `curry2(function(a, b) { return a * b; })(3)(4)` returns `12`
hints: Return a function that takes the first argument `a`. That function returns another function that takes the second argument `b` and calls the original function with both.
Use nested returns: `return function(a) { return function(b) { return fn(a, b); }; };`. Each returned function captures one argument via closure.

exercises.title: Currying: Three Arguments
exercises.description: Write a function that accepts a three-argument function and returns a curried version.
hints: Extend the `curry2` pattern by adding one more level of nesting. Each returned function captures one argument, and the innermost function calls the original with all three.
Return three levels of nested functions: `function(a) { return function(b) { return function(c) { return fn(a, b, c); }; }; }`. Each level closes over one argument.
exercises.instructions: Write a function that accepts a three-argument function and returns a curried version.

exercises.title: Partial Application
exercises.description: Write a function that accepts a two-argument function and the first argument, returning a new function that accepts the second.
hints: Partial application "locks in" the first argument and returns a function waiting for the rest. The returned function calls the original with both the fixed and new arguments.
Return `function(second) { return fn(first, second); }`. The `first` value is captured by the closure when `partial` is called.
exercises.instructions: Write a function that accepts a two-argument function and the first argument, returning a new function that accepts the second.

exercises.title: Currying: Practical Usage
exercises.description: Use currying to create a configurable string formatter that wraps a string with a prefix and suffix.
hints: This is a three-level curried function. The first call captures the prefix, the second captures the suffix, and the third concatenates them around the input string.
Return three nested functions: the innermost returns `prefix + str + suffix`. Each level closes over one argument, just like `curry3`.
exercises.instructions: Use currying to create a configurable string formatter that wraps a string with a prefix and suffix.

exercises.title: IIFE: Basics
exercises.description: Use an IIFE to create an ID generator with a private counter that returns a unique ID string each call.
exercises.instructions:
An IIFE (Immediately Invoked Function Expression) is a function that runs as soon as it is defined: `(function() { ... })()`. Variables declared inside the IIFE cannot be accessed from outside, but the returned value can still use them via closure.

Write a function that uses an IIFE internally to create a private counter. Each time the returned function is called, it increments the counter and returns an ID string in the format `"id_1"`, `"id_2"`, etc. (see `@param`/`@returns` in the starter code).

Example: `var gen = createIdGenerator(); gen()` returns `"id_1"`
Example: `gen()` returns `"id_2"` (counter increments)
Example: `var gen2 = createIdGenerator(); gen2()` returns `"id_1"` (independent counter)
hints: Wrap a function expression in parentheses and call it immediately: `(function() { ... })()`. Inside, declare a counter variable and return a function that increments and formats it.
Wrap the IIFE in parentheses and call it immediately. Inside, declare a private counter variable and return a function that increments the counter and returns a formatted string.

exercises.title: IIFE: With Parameters
exercises.description: Use an IIFE to capture a prefix configuration and return a logger with log, warn, and error methods.
hints: Pass the `prefix` as an argument to the IIFE: `(function(p) { ... })(prefix)`. Inside, return an object with `log`, `warn`, and `error` methods that use `p`.

The IIFE captures `prefix` as parameter `p`. Return `{ log: function(msg) { return p + " " + msg; }, warn: ..., error: ... }`. Each method concatenates the prefix with the appropriate label and message.
exercises.instructions: Use an IIFE to capture a prefix configuration and return a logger with log, warn, and error methods.

exercises.title: Module Pattern: Revealing
exercises.description: Use the revealing module pattern to create a calculator with private state and history tracking.
hints: Declare private variables (`result`, `history`) and private functions inside `createCalculator`. Return an object that exposes only the public methods. Use `.slice()` in `getHistory` to return a copy.
Declare private state variables for the running result and history array. Define named functions for each operation that modify the private state. Return an object whose keys map to those functions.
exercises.instructions: Use the revealing module pattern to create a calculator with private state and history tracking.

exercises.title: Module Pattern: Namespace
exercises.description: Use the module pattern to create a validator namespace with isNonEmpty, isInRange, and isValidLength methods.
hints: Create a private helper function like `trimStr` that trims whitespace. The public methods can call this shared helper internally. Return only the public methods in the object.
Define `function trimStr(str) { return str.trim(); }` as a private helper. `isNonEmpty` uses `trimStr(str).length > 0`. `isValidLength` uses both `trimStr` and `isInRange` internally.
exercises.instructions: Use the module pattern to create a validator namespace with isNonEmpty, isInRange, and isValidLength methods.

exercises.title: Module Pattern: Combined
exercises.description: Create a task manager using the module pattern with addTask, completeTask, getTasks, and getPending methods.
hints: Use a private `tasks` array. `addTask` pushes objects, `completeTask` finds the first matching undone task and sets `done` to `true`. Use `.filter()` and `.map()` for `getPending`.

For `getTasks`, return a deep-enough copy with `.map(function(t) { return { name: t.name, done: t.done }; })`. For `getPending`, chain `.filter(function(t) { return !t.done; }).map(function(t) { return t.name; })`.
exercises.instructions: Create a task manager using the module pattern with addTask, completeTask, getTasks, and getPending methods.

exercises.title: Arrow Functions: Basics
exercises.description: Write a higher-order function using arrow function syntax that applies a callback to each element of an array.
exercises.instructions:
Arrow functions are a shorter way to write functions. Instead of the `function` keyword, you use `=>`.

Full body: `const fn = (x) => { return x * 2; };`
Concise body (implicit return): `const fn = (x) => x * 2;`
Single parameter (no parens needed): `const fn = x => x * 2;`

Throughout T3 you have been writing `function()` callbacks. Now you will learn the modern equivalent.

Write a function using arrow syntax that takes an array and a callback, applies the callback to each element, and returns a new array (see `@param`/`@returns` in the starter code).

Example: `transformAll([1, 2, 3], x => x * 2)` returns `[2, 4, 6]`
Example: `transformAll(["a", "b"], s => s + "!")` returns `["a!", "b!"]`
Example: `transformAll([], x => x)` returns `[]`
hints: An arrow function uses `const name = (params) => { body };` instead of `function name(params) { body }`. Build a result array with a loop, pushing each callback result.
Use arrow function syntax for the outer function. Inside, build a result array using a loop, push each callback result, and return the array.

exercises.title: Arrow Functions: Concise Body
exercises.description: Use arrow functions with concise body (implicit return) to filter even numbers from an array.
exercises.solution: const getEvens = (nums) => nums.filter(n => n % 2 === 0);
hints: When an arrow function has a single expression, you can omit the curly braces and `return` keyword. The expression result is returned implicitly: `n => n % 2 === 0`.
Use `.filter()` with a concise arrow callback: `nums.filter(n => n % 2 === 0)`. Since this is one expression, you can write the entire function body as a single return.
exercises.instructions: Use arrow functions with concise body (implicit return) to filter even numbers from an array.

exercises.title: Arrow Functions: With Callbacks
exercises.description: Use arrow functions as callbacks to filter positive numbers and sum them in a single chained expression.
exercises.solution: const sumPositives = (nums) => nums.filter(n => n > 0).reduce((acc, n) => acc + n, 0);
hints: Chain `.filter()` and `.reduce()` with arrow callbacks. Filter keeps numbers greater than 0, then reduce sums them with an initial value of 0.
Use `nums.filter(n => n > 0).reduce((acc, n) => acc + n, 0)`. Each callback is a concise arrow function with implicit return.
exercises.instructions: Use arrow functions as callbacks to filter positive numbers and sum them in a single chained expression.

exercises.title: Arrow Functions: ES5 to ES6
exercises.description: Rewrite four ES5-style utility functions as arrow functions with concise syntax.
hints: Each function takes one parameter and returns one expression — perfect for concise arrow syntax. For a single parameter, parentheses are optional: `n => n * 2`.
Each function takes a single parameter and returns a single expression, making them ideal for concise arrow syntax. No braces or `return` needed for one-expression bodies.
exercises.instructions: Rewrite four ES5-style utility functions as arrow functions with concise syntax.

exercises.title: Arrow Functions: Lexical This
exercises.description: Create a counter object where methods use arrow functions to correctly reference the object via lexical this.
hints: Inside a `.forEach()` callback, a regular `function()` creates its own `this`, which will not point to the object. An arrow function `=>` inherits `this` from the enclosing method, where `this` is the object.

Define `addMultiple` as a regular `function` method so it receives the correct `this`. Inside that method, use an arrow callback with `.forEach()` — the arrow inherits `this` from the enclosing method.
exercises.instructions: Create a counter object where methods use arrow functions to correctly reference the object via lexical this.

exercises.title: Template Literals: Advanced
exercises.description: Use template literals with expressions to format an array of objects into a text table.
exercises.instructions:
You already know basic template literal interpolation from T1 (backticks and `${}`). At T3, you will use template literals for complex formatting tasks.

Template literals support expressions inside `${}` — not just variables but any JavaScript expression: `${score >= 60 ? "PASS" : "FAIL"}`, `${items.length}`, `${name.toUpperCase()}`.

Write a function that takes an array of `{name, score}` objects and returns a formatted string with one line per entry: `"name: score"`, joined by newlines (see `@param`/`@returns` in the starter code).

Example: `formatTable([{name: "Alice", score: 95}])` returns `"Alice: 95"`
Example: `formatTable([{name: "A", score: 1}, {name: "B", score: 2}])` returns `"A: 1\nB: 2"`
Example: `formatTable([])` returns `""`
exercises.solution: const formatTable = (entries) => entries.map(e => `${e.name}: ${e.score}`).join('\n');
hints: Use `.map()` to transform each object into a formatted string using a template literal: `` `${e.name}: ${e.score}` ``. Then `.join("\n")` to combine lines.
The full solution is a single expression: `entries.map(e => \`${e.name}: ${e.score}\`).join("\n")`. Template literals handle the interpolation, `.join()` handles the newlines.

exercises.title: Template Literals: Tagged Templates
exercises.description: Write a tagged template function that wraps each interpolated value in square brackets.
hints: A tagged template receives an array of string parts and the interpolated values as separate arguments. Loop through the strings, and after each one (except the last), insert the corresponding value wrapped in brackets.

Loop through the `strings` array by index. After appending each string part, check if there is a corresponding value at that index and insert it wrapped in brackets. The strings array is always one element longer than values.
exercises.instructions: Write a tagged template function that wraps each interpolated value in square brackets.

exercises.title: Template Literals: Builder
exercises.description: Use template literals to build an HTML string from an array of tag/content objects.
exercises.solution: const buildHTML = (elements) => elements.map(el => `<${el.tag}>${el.content}</${el.tag}>`).join('\n');
hints: Use `.map()` with a template literal to wrap each element: `` `<${el.tag}>${el.content}</${el.tag}>` ``. Join the results with newlines.
The full expression is: ``elements.map(el => `<${el.tag}>${el.content}</${el.tag}>`).join("\n")``.
exercises.instructions: Use template literals to build an HTML string from an array of tag/content objects.

exercises.title: Destructuring: Function Parameters
exercises.description: Destructure an object directly in the function parameter list with default values.
exercises.instructions:
Destructuring lets you unpack values from objects or arrays directly into variables. At T3, the most common pattern is destructuring in function parameters.

Instead of: `const formatUser = (user) => { return user.name + ", " + user.age; };`
You write: `const formatUser = ({name, age}) => { return name + ", " + age; };`

You can also set defaults for missing properties: `({name, age = 0, city = "Unknown"})`.

Write a function that destructures a user object in the parameter list and returns a formatted string (see `@param`/`@returns` in the starter code).

Example: `formatUser({name: "Alice", age: 30, city: "Seattle"})` returns `"Alice (30) - Seattle"`
Example: `formatUser({name: "Bob"})` returns `"Bob (0) - Unknown"`
exercises.solution: const formatUser = ({name, age = 0, city = "Unknown"}) => `${name} (${age}) - ${city}`;
hints: Put the destructuring pattern directly in the parameter list: `({name, age = 0, city = "Unknown"})`. Default values apply when the property is `undefined`, not when it is an empty string.
The full solution is: `const formatUser = ({name, age = 0, city = "Unknown"}) => \`${name} (${age}) - ${city}\``. Combine destructured defaults with a template literal.

exercises.title: Destructuring: Nested Objects
exercises.description: Destructure nested objects to extract deeply nested values in a function parameter.
exercises.solution: const formatAddress = ({name, address: {city, zip}}) => `${name} lives in ${city} (${zip})`;
hints: Nested destructuring follows the object shape: `{name, address: {city, zip}}` pulls `city` and `zip` from the nested `address` object. The `address` variable itself is not created.
The destructuring pattern mirrors the object structure. Use: `({name, address: {city, zip}}) => \`${name} lives in ${city} (${zip})\``.
exercises.instructions: Destructure nested objects to extract deeply nested values in a function parameter.

exercises.title: Destructuring: Array Swap and Rest
exercises.description: Use array destructuring with rest syntax to split an array into its first element and the remaining elements.
hints: Array destructuring with rest: `const [head, ...tail] = arr;` assigns the first element to `head` and collects the rest into a new array `tail`.
Use array destructuring with the rest operator to assign the first element to one variable and collect everything else. Return both as an object using shorthand property names.
exercises.instructions: Use array destructuring with rest syntax to split an array into its first element and the remaining elements.

exercises.title: Destructuring: Combined
exercises.description: Destructure a config object with nested defaults, renaming, and rest collection.
hints: Combine defaults and rest in one destructuring: `({host = "localhost", port = 3000, debug = false, ...extra})`. The `...extra` collects all properties not explicitly named.
Return using shorthand properties: `({ host, port, debug, extra })`. Parentheses around the object literal are needed for concise arrow body: `=> ({ ... })`.
exercises.instructions: Destructure a config object with nested defaults, renaming, and rest collection.

exercises.title: Rest Parameters: Collect Arguments
exercises.description: Use rest parameters to write a function that sums any number of arguments.
exercises.instructions:
In Section 2, you used the `arguments` object and a `for` loop to collect variable arguments (in `composeAll` and `pipeAll`). Rest parameters are the modern replacement.

With rest: `const sum = (...nums) => { }` — `nums` is a real array containing all arguments.
With arguments: `function sum() { var nums = []; for (var i = 0; i < arguments.length; i++) nums.push(arguments[i]); }`

Rest parameters are cleaner, work with arrow functions, and give you a real array with all array methods available.

Write a function using rest parameters that sums any number of arguments (see `@param`/`@returns` in the starter code).

Example: `sum(1, 2, 3)` returns `6`
Example: `sum()` returns `0`
Example: `sum(10)` returns `10`
exercises.solution: const sum = (...nums) => nums.reduce((acc, n) => acc + n, 0);
hints: Rest parameters (`...nums`) collect all arguments into a real array. You can immediately use `.reduce()` on it since it is a proper array.
Use `nums.reduce((acc, n) => acc + n, 0)`. The rest parameter gives you a real array, so all array methods work directly — no need for the `arguments` workaround.

exercises.title: Spread: Shallow Clone and Merge
exercises.description: Use the spread operator to merge a defaults object with user config, where user values override defaults.
exercises.solution: const mergeDefaults = (defaults, config) => ({ ...defaults, ...config });
hints: Object spread creates a shallow copy with all properties. When two objects spread into the same literal, later properties override earlier ones: `{...defaults, ...config}`.
The entire function body is: `({ ...defaults, ...config })`. Wrap in parentheses for implicit arrow return. Properties from `config` overwrite matching properties from `defaults`.
exercises.instructions: Use the spread operator to merge a defaults object with user config, where user values override defaults.

exercises.title: Spread: Array Operations
exercises.description: Use spread to insert elements into an array at a given index without mutation.
hints: Use `.slice()` to split the array at the insertion point, then spread all three parts into a new array: the before portion, the new items, and the after portion.
The pattern is: `[...arr.slice(0, index), ...items, ...arr.slice(index)]`. This creates a new array without modifying the original. Rest params in the function signature collect the items to insert.
exercises.instructions: Use spread to insert elements into an array at a given index without mutation.

exercises.title: Rest and Spread: Combined
exercises.description: Use rest to separate the first argument from the rest, then spread to build the result object.
exercises.solution: const groupFirst = (key, ...values) => ({ [key]: [...values] });
hints: Rest parameters collect extra arguments: `(key, ...values)`. Computed property names let you use a variable as a key: `{ [key]: value }`. Combine both to build the object.

The concise solution is: `({ [key]: [...values] })`. The `[key]` uses computed property syntax, `...values` spreads the rest-collected arguments into a new array. Wrap in parens for implicit arrow return.
exercises.instructions: Use rest to separate the first argument from the rest, then spread to build the result object.

exercises.title: ES6 Refactor: Callback Methods
exercises.description: Rewrite a data pipeline using arrow functions, destructuring, and template literals.
exercises.instructions:
Now you will put it all together. Rewrite familiar patterns from Sections 1 and 2 using the ES6 features you have learned.

This exercise takes an array of `{name, score}` objects and returns a summary string. Filter to passing scores (>= 60), extract the names, and join them with commas.

Use arrow functions for callbacks, destructuring in parameters, and a template literal for the result string (see `@param`/`@returns` in the starter code).

Example: `processScores([{name: "A", score: 90}, {name: "B", score: 40}, {name: "C", score: 75}])` returns `"Passing: A, C"`
Example: `processScores([{name: "A", score: 50}])` returns `"Passing: none"`
hints: Chain `.filter()` and `.map()` with arrow callbacks that destructure the parameter: `.filter(({score}) => score >= 60).map(({name}) => name)`. Use a template literal for the result.
Store the filtered names in a variable, then return `` `Passing: ${names.length > 0 ? names.join(", ") : "none"}` ``. Destructure only what you need in each callback.

exercises.title: ES6 Refactor: Closure Pattern
exercises.description: Rewrite the createCounter closure from Section 2 using const/let, arrow functions, and shorthand methods.
hints: Replace `var` with `let` for the mutable counter and `const` for the methods. Arrow functions work for the methods since they do not need their own `this`. Use shorthand property names in the return object.
Replace `var` with `let` for the mutable counter. Define each method as a `const` arrow function. Return the methods using shorthand property syntax where the key name matches the variable name.
exercises.instructions: Rewrite the createCounter closure from Section 2 using const/let, arrow functions, and shorthand methods.

exercises.title: ES6 Refactor: Composition
exercises.description: Rewrite pipeAll from Section 2 using rest parameters and arrow functions instead of arguments and var.
exercises.solution: const pipeES6 = (...fns) => (x) => fns.reduce((acc, fn) => fn(acc), x);
hints: With rest parameters, `...fns` is already a real array — no need to copy from `arguments`. Return an arrow function that reduces over `fns`.
Use rest parameters to collect all functions into a real array. Return an arrow function that calls `.reduce()` on the functions, passing each intermediate result through the next function.
exercises.instructions: Rewrite pipeAll from Section 2 using rest parameters and arrow functions instead of arguments and var.

exercises.title: ES6 Refactor: Module Pattern
exercises.description: Rewrite a task manager module using const/let, arrow functions, destructuring, and shorthand properties.
hints: This is the same logic as `createTaskManager` from Section 2, but rewritten with ES6. Use `.find()` with destructuring instead of a `for` loop for `completeTask`. Use shorthand `{ name, done: false }` and `{ addTask, completeTask, getTasks, getPending }`.
For `completeTask`, use `tasks.find(({name: n, done}) => n === name && !done)` to find the first matching undone task. Rename the destructured `name` to `n` to avoid shadowing the parameter.
exercises.instructions: Rewrite a task manager module using const/let, arrow functions, destructuring, and shorthand properties.

exercises.title: Getters and Setters
exercises.description: Create a class with a getter and setter that converts between Celsius and Fahrenheit.
hints: Store the value in `this.celsius`. The getter computes Fahrenheit using the formula `this.celsius * 9/5 + 32`. The setter converts the incoming Fahrenheit back to Celsius with `(f - 32) * 5/9`.

The `get` method computes Fahrenheit from `this.celsius` using the conversion formula. The `set` method receives a Fahrenheit value and converts it back to Celsius, storing the result in `this.celsius`.

exercises.title: Getter: Read-Only Property
exercises.description: Create a Circle class with read-only computed properties for area and circumference.
hints: Define `get area()` and `get circumference()` as getters — they look like property access (`c.area`) but compute the value each time from `this.radius`.

Use `get area() { return Math.PI * this.radius * this.radius; }` and `get circumference() { return 2 * Math.PI * this.radius; }`. Since they read `this.radius` live, they update automatically if radius changes.
exercises.instructions: Create a Circle class with read-only computed properties for area and circumference.

exercises.title: Setter: Validation
exercises.description: Create a BankAccount class with a validated setter that prevents negative balances.
hints: Store the balance in `this._balance` (the underscore signals it is private-style). The getter returns it, `deposit` adds if positive, `withdraw` subtracts only if amount is positive and does not exceed the balance.
In the constructor, use a ternary to clamp: `this._balance = initial >= 0 ? initial : 0`. For `withdraw`, check `if (amount > 0 && amount <= this._balance)` before subtracting.
exercises.instructions: Create a BankAccount class with a validated setter that prevents negative balances.

exercises.title: Static Methods
exercises.description: Create a class with static utility methods that are called on the class itself, not on instances.
hints: Static methods are defined with the `static` keyword and called on the class itself: `MathHelper.clamp(...)`. They do not have access to `this` because they are not tied to an instance.

Use `static clamp(n, min, max)` with simple conditionals. For `average`, use rest parameters and `.reduce()`: `static average(...nums) { return nums.reduce(...) / nums.length; }`. Handle the empty case.
exercises.instructions: Create a class with static utility methods that are called on the class itself, not on instances.

exercises.title: Constructor Validation
exercises.description: Create a class whose constructor validates inputs and throws errors for invalid values.
hints: Use `throw new Error("message")` in the constructor to reject invalid inputs. Check `typeof name !== "string"` or `name.trim() === ""` for the name, and `age < 0` for the age.
Check each parameter's type and value before assigning to `this`. Use `throw new Error()` to reject invalid inputs. Only assign properties after all validations pass.
exercises.instructions: Create a class whose constructor validates inputs and throws errors for invalid values.

exercises.title: Full Single Class
exercises.description: Build a complete Playlist class with methods, getters, and state management.
exercises.starterCode:
/**
 * @param {string} name - The playlist name
 * Properties: this.name, this._songs (array), this._currentIndex (starts at 0)
 * add(song) - appends a song string to the list
 * remove(song) - removes the first occurrence (adjusts index if needed)
 * next() - advances to the next song (wraps around), returns the new current song
 * get current() - returns the current song, or null if empty
 * get length() - returns the number of songs
 */
class Playlist {

}
hints: Track songs in an array and the current position with an index. `next()` increments the index and wraps with modulo: `(this._currentIndex + 1) % this._songs.length`. Handle the empty case by returning `null`.
For `remove`, find the index with `.indexOf()`, splice it out, then adjust `_currentIndex` if needed: decrement if the removed song was before the current, wrap to 0 if at the end.
exercises.instructions: Build a complete Playlist class with methods, getters, and state management.

exercises.title: Inheritance: Extends
exercises.description: Create a parent and child class using extends and super to share and override behavior.
hints: In the `Dog` constructor, call `super(name)` first — this runs the `Animal` constructor to set `this.name`. Then set `this.breed`. Override `speak()` by defining it in the `Dog` class.

Define `speak()` in both classes. `Animal` returns `"..."`. `Dog` returns `this.name + " barks"`. The child version overrides the parent. Call `super(name)` before using `this` in the child constructor.

exercises.title: Inheritance: Super with Properties
exercises.description: Create a Shape parent and Circle child class, using super to pass the color property and adding computed getters.
hints: In `Circle`, call `super(color)` to pass `color` up to the `Shape` constructor. Then set `this.radius`. Use `this.color` in `describe()` — it was set by the parent constructor.

`super(color)` runs `Shape`'s constructor which sets `this.color`. Then `this.radius = radius` adds the child-only property. The `describe()` method can access both `this.color` (inherited) and `this.radius` (own).
exercises.instructions: Create a Shape parent and Circle child class, using super to pass the color property and adding computed getters.

exercises.title: Inheritance: Method Override
exercises.description: Create Vehicle and ElectricCar classes where the child overrides a parent method.
hints: Define `fuel()` and `describe()` in both classes. The child versions override the parent versions. `ElectricCar` calls `super(make, model)` to pass both properties to `Vehicle`.
In `ElectricCar.describe()`, use `this.make`, `this.model` (inherited), and `this.range` (own) to build the string. The overridden `fuel()` simply returns `"electric"` instead of `"gasoline"`.
exercises.instructions: Create Vehicle and ElectricCar classes where the child overrides a parent method.

exercises.title: Inheritance: Shared Interface
exercises.description: Create a Notification parent class with Email and SMS children that each override the send method.
hints: All three classes share the `recipient` property through the parent. Each child calls `super(recipient)` and adds its own property. Each child overrides `send()` with its own format.

The pattern is the same for both children: call `super(recipient)`, set the extra property, override `send()`. Email uses `this.recipient` and `this.subject`. SMS uses `this.phone` and `this.recipient`.
exercises.instructions: Create a Notification parent class with Email and SMS children that each override the send method.

exercises.title: Inheritance: Combined
exercises.description: Create an Account parent and SavingsAccount child that extends with interest functionality.
exercises.starterCode:
/**
 * Account: constructor(owner, initialBalance)
 *   this.owner, this._balance (0 if initial is negative)
 *   deposit(amount) - adds if positive
 *   withdraw(amount) - subtracts if positive and sufficient funds
 *   get balance() - returns _balance
 *
 * SavingsAccount extends Account:
 *   constructor(owner, initialBalance, interestRate)
 *   this.interestRate (e.g. 0.05 for 5%)
 *   applyInterest() - adds balance * interestRate to balance
 *   get projectedBalance() - returns balance * (1 + interestRate) without modifying
 */
class Account {

}

class SavingsAccount extends Account {

}
hints: `SavingsAccount` inherits `deposit`, `withdraw`, and the `balance` getter from `Account`. It only needs to add `interestRate`, `applyInterest()`, and `projectedBalance`. Call `super(owner, initialBalance)` in the constructor.
`applyInterest()` modifies the balance: `this._balance += this._balance * this.interestRate`. The getter `projectedBalance` computes without modifying: `this._balance * (1 + this.interestRate)`.
exercises.instructions: Create an Account parent and SavingsAccount child that extends with interest functionality.

exercises.title: Class Interaction: Has-A
exercises.description: Create an Engine and Car class where Car contains an Engine and delegates to it.
exercises.instructions:
Classes often work together through composition — one class contains an instance of another. This "has-a" relationship is different from inheritance ("is-a").

A `Car` is not an `Engine`, but a `Car` has an `Engine`. The `Car` delegates engine-related behavior to its `Engine` instance.

Create an `Engine` class with `horsepower` and a `start()` method. Then create a `Car` class that takes an `Engine` in its constructor and delegates `start()` to it (see starter code).

Example: `const e = new Engine(200); const c = new Car("Toyota", e); c.start()` returns `"Toyota started with 200hp engine"`
hints: The `Car` constructor stores the `Engine` instance: `this.engine = engine`. To access the engine's power, use `this.engine.horsepower`. This is delegation — the `Car` uses the `Engine` without inheriting from it.

In `Car.start()`, build the string using `this.make` and `this.engine.horsepower`. The `hp` getter simply returns `this.engine.horsepower`. The car does not copy the value — it reads it from the engine.

exercises.title: Class Interaction: Collection
exercises.description: Create Book and Library classes where Library manages a collection of Book instances.
hints: The `Library` stores `Book` instances in an array. Use `.find()` to locate a book by title and availability status. Modify the book's `isAvailable` property directly — the library holds a reference to the same object.

For `checkout`, use `this._books.find(b => b.title === title && b.isAvailable)`. If found, set `book.isAvailable = false` and return `true`. For the `available` getter, chain `.filter()` and `.map()`.
exercises.instructions: Create Book and Library classes where Library manages a collection of Book instances.

exercises.title: Class Interaction: Delegation
exercises.description: Create Logger and App classes where App uses a Logger for all its message recording.
hints: The `App` does not log on its own — it calls `this.logger.log(...)`. Multiple apps can share the same `Logger` instance. The `messages` getter should return a copy with `.slice()` to prevent tampering.
The `App` class delegates all logging by calling `this.logger.log()` with formatted messages. In `start()` and `stop()`, update `this.isRunning` and delegate a descriptive message to the logger.
exercises.instructions: Create Logger and App classes where App uses a Logger for all its message recording.

exercises.title: Class Interaction: Builder
exercises.description: Create MenuItem and Order classes where Order manages a collection of menu items with quantities.
hints: The `add` method should check if an item with the same name already exists. If so, increment its quantity. If not, push a new entry. Use `.find()` to search by `item.name`.
For `total`, use `.reduce()` to sum `e.item.price * e.qty` across all entries. For `itemCount`, sum all `e.qty` values. For `add`, check `this._items.find(e => e.item.name === item.name)` first.
exercises.instructions: Create MenuItem and Order classes where Order manages a collection of menu items with quantities.

exercises.title: Class Interaction: Combined
exercises.description: Create Player and Inventory classes where Player has an Inventory with a weight limit.
exercises.starterCode:
/**
 * Inventory: constructor()
 *   this._items (empty array of {name, weight})
 *   add(item) - pushes {name, weight} item
 *   remove(name) - removes first item with that name
 *   has(name) - returns true if item with name exists
 *   get items() - returns copy of items array
 *   get totalWeight() - returns sum of all weights
 *
 * Player: constructor(name, maxWeight)
 *   this.name, this.maxWeight, this.inventory (new Inventory)
 *   pickup(item) - adds to inventory if totalWeight + item.weight <= maxWeight, returns true/false
 *   drop(name) - removes from inventory, returns true/false
 */
class Inventory {

}

class Player {

}
hints: The `Player` creates a new `Inventory` in its constructor. `pickup` checks the weight limit before delegating to `this.inventory.add()`. `drop` checks existence before delegating to `this.inventory.remove()`.

For `pickup`: `if (this.inventory.totalWeight + item.weight <= this.maxWeight)`. For `drop`: `if (this.inventory.has(name)) { this.inventory.remove(name); return true; }`. The Player orchestrates, the Inventory manages items.
exercises.instructions: Create Player and Inventory classes where Player has an Inventory with a weight limit.

exercises.title: Try/Catch Basics
exercises.description: Write a function that wraps a risky operation in try/catch and returns the error message on failure.
hints: Put your division logic inside `try { }`. Check if `b === 0` and `throw new Error("Cannot divide by zero")` if so. Otherwise return `a / b`. In the `catch` block, return `"Error: " + error.message`.

Your function needs three parts inside try/catch: a guard clause that throws when the divisor is zero, the normal division return, and a catch block that prefixes the error's message before returning it.

exercises.title: Finally Block
exercises.description: Write a function that uses try/catch/finally to track whether an operation was attempted, regardless of outcome.
hints: Create a `result` object with `data: null`, `error: null`, `attempted: false`. In `try`, set `result.data = JSON.parse(jsonString)`. In `catch`, set `result.error = error.message`. In `finally`, set `result.attempted = true`. Return `result`.
The `finally` block runs whether or not an error occurred. It is the right place to set `attempted: true` because it guarantees the flag is set regardless of outcome.
exercises.instructions: Write a function that uses try/catch/finally to track whether an operation was attempted, regardless of outcome.

exercises.title: Try/Catch with Return
exercises.description: Write a function that converts a string to a number, returning different values from try vs catch to handle valid and invalid input.
hints: First check `typeof value !== "string"` and throw a `TypeError`. Then use `Number(value)` and check `isNaN()`. If NaN, throw `new Error("not a number")`. In `catch`, check `error.message` to distinguish the two error cases.

The try block returns `{ value: num, status: "success" }` for valid numbers. The catch block returns `{ value: null, status: "not a number" }` if the message matches, otherwise `{ value: null, status: "error" }` for type errors.
exercises.instructions: Write a function that converts a string to a number, returning different values from try vs catch to handle valid and invalid input.

exercises.title: Throw an Error
exercises.description: Write a function that validates input and throws a descriptive Error when requirements are not met.
exercises.instructions:
The `throw` statement lets you create errors intentionally when something is wrong. This is how functions communicate that they received bad input or hit an unexpected state.

Syntax:
```
throw new Error("descriptive message");
```

When you `throw`, execution stops immediately and the error propagates up to the nearest `catch` block. If there is no catch, the program crashes — which is the correct behavior for truly invalid input.

Write `createUser(name, age)` — validate that name is a non-empty string and age is a number between 0 and 150. Throw descriptive errors for invalid input. Return an object `{ name, age }` if valid (see `@param`/`@returns` in the starter code).
hints: Check `typeof name !== "string" || name.trim() === ""` first and throw. Then check `typeof age !== "number" || age < 0 || age > 150` and throw. If both pass, return `{ name, age }`.
Use `throw new Error("Name must be a non-empty string")` for name validation and `throw new Error("Age must be a number between 0 and 150")` for age validation. Validate name before age.

exercises.title: Error Types
exercises.description: Write a function that throws the appropriate built-in error type based on what went wrong.
hints: Use `TypeError` when the wrong data type is provided (not an array, or index not a number). Use `RangeError` when a number is outside the valid range (negative or >= array length).
Check with `Array.isArray(arr)`, then `typeof index !== "number"`, then `index < 0 || index >= arr.length`. Use `throw new TypeError(...)` or `throw new RangeError(...)` accordingly.
exercises.instructions: Write a function that throws the appropriate built-in error type based on what went wrong.

exercises.title: Error Message Formatting
exercises.description: Write a function that catches errors and returns a standardized result object with success status, data, and error info.
hints: Call `operation()` inside a `try` block and capture its return value. Return `{ success: true, data: <result>, error: null }`. In `catch`, return `{ success: false, data: null, error: error.message }`.
The key insight is that `operation` is a function you call with `operation()`. Whatever it returns becomes `data`. If it throws, `error.message` becomes the error string.
exercises.instructions: Write a function that catches errors and returns a standardized result object with success status, data, and error info.

exercises.title: Custom Error Class
exercises.description: Create a custom error class that extends Error with a specific name and formatted message.
exercises.starterCode:
/**
 * Custom error class for application errors.
 *
 * @param {string} code - An error code (e.g., "NOT_FOUND", "INVALID_INPUT")
 * @param {string} message - A human-readable error description
 *
 * Properties:
 *   this.name = "AppError"
 *   this.code = code
 *   this.message = "[CODE] message"  (formatted with brackets)
 */
class AppError extends Error {

}
hints: Call `super("[" + code + "] " + message)` to set the formatted message. Then set `this.name = "AppError"` and `this.code = code`. The `extends Error` in the class declaration handles inheritance.
The constructor takes `(code, message)`. `super()` calls the Error constructor with your formatted string. After `super()`, you can set custom properties like `this.code`.

exercises.title: Validation Error
exercises.description: Create a ValidationError class that stores which field failed and what constraint was violated.
exercises.starterCode:
/**
 * Custom error for validation failures.
 *
 * @param {string} field - The name of the field that failed (e.g., "email")
 * @param {string} constraint - What was required (e.g., "must contain @")
 *
 * Properties:
 *   this.name = "ValidationError"
 *   this.field = field
 *   this.constraint = constraint
 *   this.message = "field: constraint"  (e.g., "email: must contain @")
 */
class ValidationError extends Error {

}
hints: Call `super(field + ": " + constraint)` to format the message. Then set `this.name`, `this.field`, and `this.constraint` as properties.
This follows the same pattern as AppError — extend Error, call super with a formatted string, and store extra properties. The field and constraint make it easy to identify which validation failed.
exercises.instructions: Create a ValidationError class that stores which field failed and what constraint was violated.

exercises.title: Custom Error: Combined
exercises.description: Write a function that throws different custom error types and a handler that catches and responds to each one differently.
exercises.starterCode:
/**
 * NotFoundError extends Error
 *   constructor(item) — message: "<item> not found", this.name = "NotFoundError"
 *
 * PermissionError extends Error
 *   constructor(action) — message: "Not allowed to <action>", this.name = "PermissionError"
 *
 * handleLookup(items, name, role)
 *   @param {Array<string>} items - Available items
 *   @param {string} name - Item to find
 *   @param {string} role - "admin" or "guest"
 *   @returns {string} On success: "Found: <name>"
 *
 *   If role is "guest", throw PermissionError("view items")
 *   If name is not in items, throw NotFoundError(name)
 *
 * handleErrors(items, name, role)
 *   Calls handleLookup inside try/catch.
 *   If NotFoundError: return "Missing: <error.message>"
 *   If PermissionError: return "Denied: <error.message>"
 *   If any other error: return "Unknown error"
 *   On success: return the result from handleLookup
 */
hints: Create two error classes extending Error. In `handleErrors`, use `instanceof` to check which type of error was caught: `if (error instanceof NotFoundError)` vs `if (error instanceof PermissionError)`.

In `handleLookup`, check role first (throw PermissionError), then check if name is in items (throw NotFoundError). In `handleErrors`, wrap `handleLookup()` in try/catch and use `instanceof` to format different responses.
exercises.instructions: Write a function that throws different custom error types and a handler that catches and responds to each one differently.

exercises.title: Parse or Default
exercises.description: Write a function that attempts to parse data and returns a default value on failure instead of crashing.
hints: Wrap `JSON.parse(jsonString)` in a `try` block and return the result. In the `catch` block, return `defaultValue`. This is one of the most common try/catch patterns.
The entire function is just: `try { return JSON.parse(jsonString); } catch (error) { return defaultValue; }`. The catch block ignores the error details and just falls back.
exercises.instructions: Write a function that attempts to parse data and returns a default value on failure instead of crashing.

exercises.title: Safe Wrapper
exercises.description: Write a higher-order function that wraps any function in try/catch and returns a safe version that never throws.
hints: Return a new function that uses `...args` to accept any arguments. Inside it, call `fn(...args)` inside a `try` block. This combines higher-order functions (Section 2) with error handling.

Return a new function that accepts any arguments using rest parameters. Inside that function, wrap the original function call in try/catch. On success, return an object with a truthy status and the data. On failure, return an object with a falsy status and the error message.
exercises.instructions: Write a higher-order function that wraps any function in try/catch and returns a safe version that never throws.

exercises.title: Error Handling: Combined
exercises.description: Write a config loader that uses custom errors, validation, and try/catch to handle multiple failure modes gracefully.
exercises.starterCode:
/**
 * ConfigError extends Error
 *   constructor(key, reason) — message: "Config error [key]: reason"
 *   this.name = "ConfigError", this.key = key
 *
 * loadConfig(jsonString)
 *   @param {string} jsonString - JSON string of config data
 *   @returns {{ success: boolean, config: object|null, errors: string[] }}
 *
 *   1. Parse jsonString (if invalid JSON, return { success: false, config: null, errors: ["Invalid JSON: <parse error message>"] })
 *   2. Validate required keys: "host" (string), "port" (number 1-65535)
 *      For each missing/invalid key, collect a ConfigError (don't stop at the first)
 *   3. If errors collected: return { success: false, config: null, errors: [<error messages>] }
 *   4. If valid: return { success: true, config: { host, port }, errors: [] }
 */
hints: First try to parse the JSON — if that fails, return immediately with the parse error. Then validate each field and collect ConfigError instances into an array. After all checks, return based on whether errors were collected.

Start by attempting to parse the JSON inside try/catch — return the failure object immediately if parsing fails. After parsing, validate each config field independently, collecting any errors into an array. At the end, check the array length to decide whether to return success or failure.
exercises.instructions: Write a config loader that uses custom errors, validation, and try/catch to handle multiple failure modes gracefully.

exercises.title: getElementById
exercises.description: Write a function that finds an element by its ID and returns its text content.
exercises.instructions:
The DOM (Document Object Model) is how JavaScript connects to HTML. The browser converts your HTML into a tree of objects — each element becomes a "node" you can find, read, and change with JavaScript.

`document.getElementById(id)` finds a single element by its `id` attribute. It returns the element object, or `null` if no element has that ID.

Once you have an element, `element.textContent` gives you all the text inside it.

Syntax:
```
const el = document.getElementById("myId");
el.textContent; // "the text inside"
```

Write `getTextById(id)` — find the element with the given ID and return its text content. If no element is found, return `null` (see `@param`/`@returns` in the starter code).
hints: Use `document.getElementById(id)` to find the element. Check if the result is `null` before accessing `.textContent`. Return `null` if no element is found.
Look up the element using `getElementById`, then check whether the result is `null` before trying to access `textContent`. Return `null` for missing elements and the text content for found ones.

exercises.title: querySelector
exercises.description: Write a function that uses a CSS selector to find an element and return its text content.
hints: `document.querySelector(selector)` works just like CSS selectors — `.class`, `#id`, `tag`, `[attribute]`, and even combined selectors like `#nav li`. It returns the first match or `null`.
The approach mirrors `getElementById` but uses `querySelector` instead. Find the element, handle the `null` case, and return `textContent` if the element exists.
exercises.instructions: Write a function that uses a CSS selector to find an element and return its text content.

exercises.title: querySelectorAll
exercises.description: Write a function that selects all matching elements and returns an array of their text content.
hints: `querySelectorAll` returns a NodeList, not an Array. Convert it with `Array.from(nodeList)` or `[...nodeList]`, then use `.map()` to extract each element's `.textContent`.
Convert the `NodeList` from `querySelectorAll` into a real array, then use `.map()` to extract `textContent` from each element.
exercises.instructions: Write a function that selects all matching elements and returns an array of their text content.

exercises.title: Change Text Content
exercises.description: Write a function that updates the text content of an element found by ID.
exercises.instructions:
Reading from the DOM is only half the story — you can also change elements. Setting `element.textContent` replaces all the text inside an element.

Syntax:
```
const el = document.getElementById("greeting");
el.textContent = "Hello!"; // replaces the text
```

This is one-way: setting `textContent` removes any existing child elements and replaces everything with plain text. It's the safest way to set text because it won't accidentally inject HTML.

Write `setText(id, text)` — find the element by ID and set its text content (see `@param` in the starter code).
hints: Find the element with `document.getElementById(id)`, then set `element.textContent = text`. Check that the element exists before setting to avoid errors with invalid IDs.
Find the element by ID first, then guard against `null` before setting `textContent`. Only update the text when the element actually exists in the DOM.

exercises.title: Modify Styles
exercises.description: Write a function that changes an inline style property on an element.
hints: Access inline styles with `element.style[property]` using bracket notation (since the property name is a variable). CSS properties use camelCase in JavaScript: `background-color` becomes `backgroundColor`.
After finding the element by ID, use bracket notation on the `style` object to set the property dynamically, since the property name comes in as a variable rather than a fixed string.
exercises.instructions: Write a function that changes an inline style property on an element.

exercises.title: classList
exercises.description: Write a function that adds, removes, or toggles a CSS class on an element and reports whether the class is present.
hints: Use `element.classList.add(className)`, `.remove(className)`, or `.toggle(className)` based on the action. After the operation, `element.classList.contains(className)` tells you if the class is present.
Use an if/else chain to pick the right `classList` method based on the action parameter. After performing the action, use `classList.contains()` to check and return whether the class is present.
exercises.instructions: Write a function that adds, removes, or toggles a CSS class on an element and reports whether the class is present.

exercises.title: Set Attributes
exercises.description: Write a function that sets an attribute on an element and another that reads an attribute value.
hints: `element.setAttribute(attr, value)` sets any attribute. `element.getAttribute(attr)` reads it back (returns `null` if the attribute doesn't exist). These work for standard attributes like `href` and custom ones like `data-*`.
For `setAttr`: find element, call `element.setAttribute(attr, value)`. For `getAttr`: find element, return `element.getAttribute(attr)`. Handle missing elements by returning `null`.
exercises.instructions: Write a function that sets an attribute on an element and another that reads an attribute value.

exercises.title: Create and Append
exercises.description: Write a function that creates a new element with text and appends it to a container.
exercises.instructions:
You can create brand-new HTML elements with JavaScript and add them to the page.

`document.createElement(tag)` creates a new element (not yet on the page).
`element.textContent = "..."` sets its text.
`parent.appendChild(child)` places it inside a parent element.

Syntax:
```
const p = document.createElement("p");
p.textContent = "New paragraph";
document.getElementById("container").appendChild(p);
```

The new element only appears on the page after `appendChild`. Until then, it exists in memory but is invisible.

Write `createAndAppend(tag, text, parentId)` — create an element of the given tag, set its text, and append it to the parent (see `@param`/`@returns` in the starter code).
hints: Three steps: `document.createElement(tag)` creates it, `element.textContent = text` fills it, `document.getElementById(parentId).appendChild(element)` places it. Return the element.
Follow the three-step pattern: create the element with `createElement`, set its `textContent`, then attach it to the parent using `appendChild`. Return the newly created element at the end.

exercises.title: Build a List
exercises.description: Write a function that creates a ul element with li children from an array and appends it to a container.
hints: Create the `<ul>` first with `document.createElement("ul")`. Then loop through the items array, creating a `<li>` for each. Append each `<li>` to the `<ul>`, then append the `<ul>` to the container.

Create the list container element first, then iterate over the items array to create and append child elements to it. After building all the children, append the complete list to the container and return it.
exercises.instructions: Write a function that creates a ul element with li children from an array and appends it to a container.

exercises.title: Remove Elements
exercises.description: Write a function that removes all elements matching a CSS selector and returns how many were removed.
hints: Use `document.querySelectorAll(selector)` to find all matches. Save the count before removing. Call `.remove()` on each element. The `forEach` method works on NodeList too.
Select all matching elements with `querySelectorAll`, save the count before removing anything, then iterate and call `remove()` on each element. Return the count you saved.
exercises.instructions: Write a function that removes all elements matching a CSS selector and returns how many were removed.

exercises.title: Click Handler
exercises.description: Write a function that sets up a click counter — each button click increments and displays a count.
hints: Declare a `let count = 0` variable. Set the display text to `"0"`. Inside the click listener, increment `count` and update `display.textContent`. The listener creates a closure over `count`.
Declare a counter variable outside the listener to form a closure. Initialize the display, then inside the click listener, increment the counter and update the display with the new value.

exercises.title: Event Object
exercises.description: Write a function that reports which button was clicked using the event object.
hints: Use `container.querySelectorAll("button")` to find all buttons, then loop with `.forEach()` to attach a click listener to each. Inside the listener, `event.target.textContent` gives you the clicked button's text.

Select all buttons inside the container and attach a click listener to each one. Inside the listener, use the event parameter to read the content of whichever button was actually clicked, then display it in the output element.
exercises.instructions: Write a function that reports which button was clicked using the event object.

exercises.title: Form Submit
exercises.description: Write a function that handles form submission by preventing the default action, reading the input, and displaying a greeting.
exercises.starterCode:
/**
 * @param {string} formId - ID of the form element
 * @param {string} outputId - ID of the element to display the greeting
 * When the form is submitted:
 * 1. Prevent the default form submission
 * 2. Read the value from the input with name="username"
 * 3. Set the output text to "Hello, <username>!"
 * 4. Clear the input value
 */
function setupForm(formId, outputId) {

}
