hints: Listen for the `"submit"` event on the form. Call `event.preventDefault()` to stop the page from reloading. Read the input with `form.querySelector('input[name="username"]').value`. Clear the input by setting `.value = ""`.

Listen for the `submit` event on the form. Inside the handler, prevent the default page reload, read the input value using a name-attribute selector, update the output text with a greeting, and clear the input afterward.
exercises.instructions: Write a function that handles form submission by preventing the default action, reading the input, and displaying a greeting.

exercises.title: DOM and Events: Combined
exercises.description: Write a function that creates list items from user input — combining element creation, event handling, and DOM manipulation.
exercises.starterCode:
/**
 * @param {string} inputId - ID of the text input
 * @param {string} buttonId - ID of the "Add" button
 * @param {string} listId - ID of the <ul> to append items to
 * When the button is clicked:
 * 1. Read the input value
 * 2. If not empty, create a <li> with that text and append to the list
 * 3. Clear the input after adding
 * If the input is empty, do nothing.
 */
function setupListAdder(inputId, buttonId, listId) {

}
hints: Attach a `"click"` listener to the button. Inside, read `input.value`, check if it's empty (after trimming), create a `<li>` with `document.createElement`, set its text, append it to the list, and clear the input.

Inside the button's click listener, read and trim the input value, skip empty strings, create a new list item element with the text, append it to the list, and clear the input. Combine element creation with the event pattern.
exercises.instructions: Write a function that creates list items from user input — combining element creation, event handling, and DOM manipulation.

exercises.title: Create a Promise
exercises.description: Write a function that returns a Promise which resolves or rejects based on a condition.
exercises.instructions:
A **Promise** represents a value that may not be available yet. You create one with `new Promise((resolve, reject) => { ... })`.

- Call `resolve(value)` when the operation succeeds — the Promise becomes "fulfilled" with that value.
- Call `reject(error)` when it fails — the Promise becomes "rejected" with that error.

A Promise is always in one of three states: **pending** (not yet settled), **fulfilled** (resolved), or **rejected**.

Write `makePromise(value)` — return a new Promise that resolves with `value` if it is truthy, or rejects with a new Error "Empty value" if it is falsy (see `@param`/`@returns` in the starter code).
exercises.hint1: Think about what makes a value "truthy" in JavaScript — everything except `false`, `0`, `""`, `null`, `undefined`, and `NaN`. Inside the Promise constructor callback, check the value and call either `resolve` or `reject`.
exercises.hint2: The Promise constructor takes a function with two parameters: `resolve` and `reject`. Use an `if` statement to check if `value` is truthy — if so, call `resolve(value)`, otherwise call `reject(new Error("Empty value"))`.
hints: A Promise is created with `new Promise(function(resolve, reject) { ... })`. Inside that callback, you decide whether to call `resolve` or `reject` based on whether the input passes a truthiness check.
Return a new Promise. Inside the executor, use a conditional to test the value — call `resolve()` with the value for the success path and `reject()` with a `new Error(...)` for the failure path.

exercises.title: Promise Chaining
exercises.description: Write a function that chains .then() calls to transform a resolved value through multiple steps.
exercises.hint1: `.then()` takes a callback that receives the resolved value and returns a new value (or Promise). Each `.then()` returns a new Promise, so you can chain them. `Promise.resolve(value)` creates a Promise that is already resolved.
exercises.hint2: Start with `Promise.resolve(num)` to wrap the number in a Promise. Chain `.then(function(n) { return n * 2; })` to double it, then another `.then()` to prepend "Result: " to the doubled value.
exercises.instructions: Write a function that chains .then() calls to transform a resolved value through multiple steps.
hints: Promise chaining lets you transform a value step by step. Each `.then()` receives the return value of the previous `.then()` and passes its own return value to the next one in the chain.
Start with `Promise.resolve(num)` to wrap the number. Chain two `.then()` calls — one to perform the arithmetic, another to build the labeled string.

exercises.title: Promise Rejection
exercises.description: Write a function that uses .catch() to handle a rejected Promise and return a fallback value.
exercises.hint1: `.catch()` is called only when the Promise rejects — it receives the rejection reason and can return a new value, which becomes the resolved value of the resulting Promise. If the Promise resolves normally, `.catch()` is skipped entirely.
exercises.hint2: Chain `.catch()` onto the promise parameter. Inside the `.catch()` callback, ignore the error argument and simply return the `fallback` value. The resolved case passes through automatically.
exercises.instructions: Write a function that uses .catch() to handle a rejected Promise and return a fallback value.
hints: The `.catch()` method attaches a handler that runs only when a Promise rejects. Whatever value you return from `.catch()` becomes the new resolved value of the chain.
Chain `.catch()` on the incoming promise. Inside the handler, return the `fallback` parameter. The resolved path passes through `.catch()` untouched.

exercises.title: Promise: Combined
exercises.description: Write a function that chains .then() transformations with a .catch() fallback to safely process a Promise.
exercises.hint1: Chain `.then()` calls for the success path (triple the number, then add the prefix). Add `.catch()` at the end to handle the rejection path. If any `.then()` in the chain throws or the original Promise rejects, control jumps to `.catch()`.
exercises.hint2: Start with `promise.then(function(n) { return n * 3; })` to triple the value. Chain another `.then()` to prepend "Value: ". Then add `.catch(function(err) { return "Error: " + err.message; })` at the end.
exercises.instructions: Write a function that chains .then() transformations with a .catch() fallback to safely process a Promise.
hints: You can chain `.then()` for transformations and add `.catch()` at the end for error handling. If the original Promise rejects, control skips the `.then()` calls and jumps straight to `.catch()`.
Chain the promise through two `.then()` steps for the success path — one for the arithmetic and one for the string prefix. Add `.catch()` at the end to handle rejections using `err.message`.

exercises.title: async Function Basics
exercises.description: Write an async function that awaits a Promise and returns the transformed result.
exercises.hint1: Use `await` to get the string value out of the Promise, then apply `.toUpperCase()` to the result. Because the function is `async`, the return value is automatically wrapped in a Promise.
exercises.hint2: Inside the function body: `const str = await promise;` unwraps the string from the Promise. Then `return str.toUpperCase();` converts and returns it.
hints: An `async` function always returns a Promise. Inside it, `await` pauses execution until a Promise resolves, giving you the resolved value directly as a regular variable.
Use `await` to unwrap the string from the promise, then apply a string method to transform it before returning.

exercises.title: Await Sequential
exercises.description: Write an async function that awaits two Promises in sequence and combines their results.
exercises.hint1: Use `await` twice — once for each Promise — to get both values before combining them. The `await` keyword pauses the function until each Promise resolves, so you can work with the values like normal variables.
exercises.hint2: `const a = await promiseA;` and `const b = await promiseB;` give you both numbers. Then return an object with `sum: a + b`, `product: a * b`, and `larger` using a ternary or `Math.max`.
exercises.instructions: Write an async function that awaits two Promises in sequence and combines their results.
hints: You can `await` multiple Promises one after another, storing each result in a variable. This lets you use both resolved values together to build your return value.
Await each promise into its own variable. Then return an object whose properties are computed from those two values — addition, multiplication, and a comparison to find the greater one.

exercises.title: Async Error Handling
exercises.description: Write an async function that uses try/catch to handle a rejected Promise gracefully.
exercises.hint1: When you `await` a rejected Promise inside a `try` block, it throws an error that gets caught by the `catch` block — the same try/catch you learned in error handling, but now with async code.
exercises.hint2: Wrap `const data = await promise;` in a `try` block and return the success object. In the `catch(err)` block, return the error object using `err.message`.
exercises.instructions: Write an async function that uses try/catch to handle a rejected Promise gracefully.
hints: Wrapping `await` in a try/catch block lets you handle rejected Promises the same way you handle thrown errors. The try block handles success; the catch block handles failure.
In the `try` block, `await` the promise and return an object indicating success with the resolved data. In the `catch` block, return an object indicating failure with the error's `.message` property.

exercises.title: async/await: Combined
exercises.description: Write an async function that awaits multiple Promises sequentially with error handling, collecting successes and failures.
exercises.hint1: Loop through the promises array and `await` each one inside a `try/catch`. Push resolved values into one array and error messages into another. A `for` loop works well here since you need `await` inside it.
exercises.hint2: Create `values` and `errors` arrays. Use `for (let i = 0; i < promises.length; i++)` and inside: `try { const val = await promises[i]; values.push(val); } catch (err) { errors.push(err.message); }`. Return both arrays in an object.
exercises.instructions: Write an async function that awaits multiple Promises sequentially with error handling, collecting successes and failures.
hints: Loop through the array of promises one at a time. For each promise, use try/catch with `await` — successes go in one collection, failures in another.

Use a `for` loop (not `.forEach()`, since you need `await`). Inside each iteration, try to await the promise and collect the value on success, or collect `err.message` on failure. Return both collections in an object.

exercises.title: Promisify a Callback
exercises.description: Write a function that converts a callback-style function into one that returns a Promise.
exercises.hint1: The callback convention is `(error, result)` — if `error` is truthy the operation failed, otherwise `result` holds the value. Your promisified version should map this pattern onto `reject`/`resolve`.
exercises.hint2: Return a new function that takes `value` and returns `new Promise(function(resolve, reject) { callbackFn(value, function(error, result) { if (error) reject(error); else resolve(result); }); });`.
exercises.instructions: Write a function that converts a callback-style function into one that returns a Promise.
hints: Promisifying means wrapping a callback-style function inside a new Promise. The Node-style callback pattern is `(error, result)` — error means failure, result means success.
Return a new function that returns a `new Promise(...)`. Inside the Promise executor, call the original `callbackFn` and provide a callback that maps `error` to `reject` and `result` to `resolve`.

exercises.title: Async Pipeline
exercises.description: Write an async function that passes a value through an array of async transform functions in sequence.
exercises.hint1: This is the async version of the `pipe` pattern you learned in advanced functions. Loop through the transforms array, awaiting each one and passing the result to the next. If the array is empty, just return the initial value.
exercises.hint2: Start with `let result = initial;`. Use a `for` loop over `transforms` and inside: `result = await transforms[i](result);`. After the loop, `return result;`.
exercises.instructions: Write an async function that passes a value through an array of async transform functions in sequence.
hints: A pipeline passes a value through a series of transformations in order. Each transform function is async, so you need to `await` its result before passing it to the next one.

Keep a running `result` variable starting with the initial value. Loop through the `transforms` array and in each iteration, reassign `result` to the awaited return of the current transform. Return the final result.

exercises.title: Application: Generate Report Cards
exercises.description: Write a function that transforms an array of student records into report card objects with averages and letter grades.
exercises.hint1: Use `.map()` to transform each student, and `.reduce()` inside to sum their scores. Divide by `scores.length` for the average. Use `Math.round(value * 10) / 10` to round to one decimal place.
exercises.hint2: Destructure `{ name, scores }` in the map callback. Compute `average` with reduce, then use if/else if chains for the letter grade thresholds (90=A, 80=B, 70=C, 60=D, else F). Return an object with all four properties.
exercises.instructions: Write a function that transforms an array of student records into report card objects with averages and letter grades.
hints: For each student, calculate the average of their scores array, then determine the letter grade using threshold checks. Round the average to one decimal place with the multiply-round-divide pattern.

Use `.map()` on the students array. Inside, compute the average with `.reduce()` and division, then use if/else-if chains for letter grade thresholds. Set the `passing` flag based on whether the average meets the cutoff.

exercises.title: Application: Analyze Sales Data
exercises.description: Write a function that analyzes an array of sales records and returns a summary with total revenue, category totals, and the best-selling product.
exercises.hint1: Use `.reduce()` three times: once for total revenue (sum of quantity * price), once to build an object of category totals, and once to build an object of product totals. Then find the product with the highest total.
exercises.hint2: For category/product totals, use the pattern: `acc[key] = (acc[key] || 0) + revenue`. For best seller, use `Object.keys(productRevenue).reduce()` to find the key with the highest value.
exercises.instructions: Write a function that analyzes an array of sales records and returns a summary with total revenue, category totals, and the best-selling product.
hints: Break this into three aggregations: total revenue is the sum of quantity times price; category totals group revenue by category key; best seller is the product with the highest cumulative revenue.

Use `.reduce()` to accumulate totals into objects keyed by category and by product. The accumulator pattern `acc[key] = (acc[key] || 0) + amount` handles new keys. Find the best seller by comparing values across the per-product object.

exercises.title: Application: Build Search Index
exercises.description: Write a function that builds a word-to-titles index from an array of documents, mapping each lowercase word to the titles that contain it.
exercises.hint1: Use `.reduce()` over the docs array to build an index object. For each doc, split the body into words (lowercase), then for each word add the title to the index if not already present. Use `.indexOf()` to check for duplicates.
exercises.hint2: Start with `docs.reduce(function(index, doc) { ... }, {})`. Inside, split `doc.body.toLowerCase()` on whitespace. For each word, create the array if needed (`if (!index[word]) index[word] = []`) then push the title if `indexOf(doc.title) === -1`.
exercises.instructions: Write a function that builds a word-to-titles index from an array of documents, mapping each lowercase word to the titles that contain it.
hints: For each document, split its body into lowercase words and associate each word with the document's title. The index maps words to arrays of titles, and the same title should not appear twice for the same word.

Use `.reduce()` to build the index object. For each doc, lowercase and split the body on whitespace. For each word, ensure an array exists at that key and add the title only if it is not already present.

exercises.title: Application: Tournament Rankings
exercises.description: Write a function that ranks tournament players by win rate, filters by minimum games played, and formats the results as ranked strings.
exercises.hint1: Chain four array methods: `.filter()` by minimum games, `.map()` to compute win rates, `.sort()` by win rate descending, then `.map()` again to format as ranked strings. Use `Math.round(rate * 10) / 10` for one decimal.
exercises.hint2: Filter: `(p.wins + p.losses) >= minGames`. First map: `{ player, winRate: wins/(wins+losses)*100 }`. Sort: `b.winRate - a.winRate`. Second map: `"#" + (i+1) + " " + p.player + " (" + rounded + "%)"` where `i` is the index parameter.
exercises.instructions: Write a function that ranks tournament players by win rate, filters by minimum games played, and formats the results as ranked strings.
hints: This is a filter-map-sort-map pipeline: first exclude players below the games threshold, then compute win rates, sort by rate descending, and format each entry with a ranking number.

Filter where total games meets the minimum, map to objects with a computed win-rate percentage, sort descending, then map again to formatted strings. Use the `.map()` callback's index parameter for the ranking number. Round rates to one decimal.

exercises.title: Application: Bank Account
exercises.description: Write a BankAccount class with deposit, withdraw, and transfer methods, plus overdraft protection and a transaction history.
exercises.starterCode:
/**
 * BankAccount class
 * @param {string} owner - Account owner name
 * @param {number} [balance=0] - Starting balance
 *
 * Methods:
 *   deposit(amount) - Add funds, throw Error("Invalid amount") if amount <= 0
 *   withdraw(amount) - Remove funds, throw Error("Invalid amount") if <= 0, Error("Insufficient funds") if > balance
 *   transfer(amount, otherAccount) - Withdraw from this, deposit to other
 *
 * Properties:
 *   get balance - Current balance
 *   get history - Array of { type: "deposit"|"withdraw"|"transfer", amount } objects
 */
exercises.hint1: Store balance and history as private properties (prefix with `_`). Use a getter for `balance` and `history`. The `transfer` method can call `this.withdraw()` then `otherAccount.deposit()` to reuse validation logic.
exercises.hint2: In `withdraw`, check `amount <= 0` first (throw "Invalid amount"), then `amount > this._balance` (throw "Insufficient funds"). For `transfer`, call withdraw and deposit, then update the last history entry's type to "transfer".
exercises.instructions: Write a BankAccount class with deposit, withdraw, and transfer methods, plus overdraft protection and a transaction history.
hints: A class with private state uses underscore-prefixed properties and exposes them through getters. Each method modifies internal state and records the action in a history array.

Store `_balance` and `_history` in the constructor. Validate amounts in `deposit` and `withdraw` before modifying state. The `transfer` method can reuse `withdraw` and `deposit` internally, then update the most recent history entry's type.

exercises.title: Application: Event Emitter
exercises.description: Write an EventEmitter class that allows subscribing to named events, emitting events with data, and removing listeners.
exercises.starterCode:
/**
 * EventEmitter class
 *
 * Methods:
 *   on(event, listener) - Register a listener function for the named event
 *   emit(event, ...args) - Call all listeners for the event with the given arguments; returns number of listeners called
 *   off(event, listener) - Remove a specific listener from the event
 *   listenerCount(event) - Return the number of listeners for the event
 */
exercises.hint1: Store listeners in an object where keys are event names and values are arrays of listener functions. `on` pushes to the array, `emit` loops through and calls each one, `off` finds and removes a specific function reference.
exercises.hint2: Use `this._events = {}` in the constructor. For `emit`, get the listeners array, return 0 if none. Otherwise loop with `.forEach()` and call each listener with the extra arguments. For `off`, use `.indexOf()` and `.splice()` to remove.
exercises.instructions: Write an EventEmitter class that allows subscribing to named events, emitting events with data, and removing listeners.
hints: An EventEmitter stores listeners in an object keyed by event name, where each key maps to an array of callback functions. Emitting calls every listener for that event; removing deletes a specific one.

Initialize `this._events = {}` in the constructor. `on()` creates or appends to the array. `emit()` iterates over listeners and calls each with the provided arguments. `off()` locates the function reference in the array and removes it.

exercises.title: Application: Validator Builder
exercises.description: Write a createValidator function that builds chainable validators by composing rule functions.
exercises.hint1: Create a `rules` array via closure. Each chainable method pushes a validation function to `rules` and returns the validator object for chaining. `.validate()` runs all rules and collects non-null error strings.
exercises.hint2: Each rule function takes the value and returns an error string or null. For chaining, each method returns the same `validator` object. In `.validate()`, map rules to results, filter out nulls, and return `{ valid, errors }`.
exercises.instructions: Write a createValidator function that builds chainable validators by composing rule functions.
hints: A chainable API works by having each method return the same object. Collect rule functions in an array via closure, and when `validate()` is called, run all rules against the value to collect errors.

Each method like `required()`, `minLength(n)`, etc. pushes a rule function to the array and returns the validator object. Each rule function takes the value and returns either an error string or `null`. The `validate()` method runs all rules and filters out the nulls.

exercises.title: Application: Memoize Function
exercises.description: Write a memoize function that caches the results of a function based on its arguments, avoiding redundant computation.
exercises.hint1: Use a `Map` for the cache, with `JSON.stringify(arguments)` as the key. Before calling the original function, check if the key exists in the cache. Attach the cache as a `.cache` property on the returned function.
exercises.hint2: Convert arguments to an array, then stringify for the key: `JSON.stringify(Array.prototype.slice.call(arguments))`. If `cache.has(key)`, return `cache.get(key)`. Otherwise call `fn`, store the result with `cache.set(key, result)`, and return it.
exercises.instructions: Write a memoize function that caches the results of a function based on its arguments, avoiding redundant computation.
hints: Memoization caches function results so repeated calls with the same arguments skip recomputation. Use a `Map` for the cache, with serialized arguments as the key.

Return a wrapper function that serializes its arguments into a cache key. If the key exists in the `Map`, return the cached value. Otherwise, call the original function, store the result, and return it. Expose the `Map` as a `.cache` property on the wrapper.

exercises.title: Application: Click Counter Widget
exercises.description: Write a function that creates a click counter widget — a button and a display element that shows how many times the button has been clicked.
exercises.hint1: Use a closure variable `count` to track clicks. Get the button and display elements by ID, set the initial text, then add a "click" event listener that increments the counter and updates the display.
exercises.hint2: Declare `let count = 0;` inside the function. Use `document.getElementById()` for both elements. Set `display.textContent = "Clicks: 0"`. Add `button.addEventListener("click", function() { count++; display.textContent = "Clicks: " + count; })`.
exercises.instructions: Write a function that creates a click counter widget — a button and a display element that shows how many times the button has been clicked.
hints: Use a closure variable to track the click count. Get references to the button and display elements, set the initial text, then listen for click events to update both the counter and the display.

Declare a counter variable inside the function. Use `document.getElementById()` to get both elements. Set the display's initial `textContent`, then add a `"click"` event listener that increments the counter and updates the display text.

exercises.title: Application: Dynamic Table Builder
exercises.description: Write a function that generates an HTML table from an array of objects, using the object keys as column headers.
exercises.hint1: Get the keys from the first object with `Object.keys(data[0])`. Create `<table>`, `<thead>`, and `<tbody>` elements. Loop through keys for `<th>` headers, then loop through data for `<tr>` rows with `<td>` cells.
exercises.hint2: Use `document.createElement()` for each element. For headers: loop keys, create `<th>`, set `textContent`, append to header row. For body: loop data, create `<tr>`, loop keys for each `<td>` with `row[key]` as textContent. Append table to container.
exercises.instructions: Write a function that generates an HTML table from an array of objects, using the object keys as column headers.
hints: Building a table from data requires creating the DOM structure: `<table>` with `<thead>` for column headers and `<tbody>` for data rows. Extract column names from the keys of the first object.

Use `Object.keys(data[0])` for column names. Create header cells (`<th>`) inside a `<tr>` in `<thead>`. Then loop over the data array to create body rows, with a `<td>` for each key's value. Handle the empty-data edge case.

exercises.title: Application: Filterable List
exercises.description: Write a function that sets up a text input to filter a list of items — typing in the input hides list items that do not match (case-insensitive).
exercises.hint1: Add an "input" event listener on the text input. Inside, get the search value (lowercased), select all `<li>` elements inside the list, and toggle each one's `style.display` based on whether its `textContent` includes the search text.
exercises.hint2: Use `input.addEventListener("input", ...)`. Inside: `const search = input.value.toLowerCase()`. Then `list.querySelectorAll("li").forEach(...)` — for each item, check `item.textContent.toLowerCase().indexOf(search) !== -1`. Set `style.display` to `""` or `"none"`.
exercises.instructions: Write a function that sets up a text input to filter a list of items — typing in the input hides list items that do not match (case-insensitive).
hints: Filtering a list means listening for text input changes, then looping through all list items and comparing their content to the search term case-insensitively. Non-matching items get hidden via `style.display`.

Add an `"input"` event listener on the text field. Inside, lowercase the search value, then iterate over all `<li>` elements in the list. For each item, check if its lowercased text content contains the search string and toggle its `display` style accordingly.

exercises.title: Application: Retry Until Success
exercises.description: Write an async function that retries a failing async operation up to a maximum number of times before giving up.
exercises.hint1: Use a `for` loop from 0 to maxRetries (inclusive). Inside, `try` to `await asyncFn()` and return on success. In `catch`, save the error. After the loop ends without returning, throw a new Error with the attempt count and last error message.
exercises.hint2: Loop `for (let i = 0; i <= maxRetries; i++)`. Inside: `try { return await asyncFn(); } catch (err) { lastError = err; }`. After the loop: `throw new Error("Failed after " + (maxRetries + 1) + " attempts: " + lastError.message)`.
exercises.instructions: Write an async function that retries a failing async operation up to a maximum number of times before giving up.
hints: A retry function attempts the async operation, and if it fails, tries again up to a maximum count. Keep track of the last error so you can include it in the final failure message.

Use a `for` loop that runs `maxRetries + 1` total iterations (initial try + retries). In each iteration, try to `await` the function and return on success, or save the error on failure. After the loop exhausts all attempts, throw a new Error with the attempt count and last error's message.

exercises.title: Application: Config Loader
exercises.description: Write an async function that tries multiple config sources in order and returns the first successful result.
exercises.hint1: Loop through the sources array and `await` each one inside a `try/catch`. If it succeeds, return immediately. If it fails, continue to the next source. If the loop finishes without returning, throw the "All config sources failed" error.
exercises.hint2: Use `for (let i = 0; i < sources.length; i++)` with `try { return await sources[i](); } catch (err) { }` inside. After the loop: `throw new Error("All config sources failed");`. The early `return` ensures you stop at the first success.
exercises.instructions: Write an async function that tries multiple config sources in order and returns the first successful result.
hints: Try each config source in order — if one fails, skip to the next. The first one that succeeds provides your config. If none succeed, report failure.

Loop through the `sources` array with a `for` loop. Use try/catch around `await sources[i]()` — return immediately on success, silently continue on failure. After the loop ends without returning, throw an error indicating all sources failed.

exercises.title: Application: Async Data Pipeline
exercises.description: Write an async function that processes data through a pipeline of async stages (fetch, transform, validate), with error handling at each step.
exercises.hint1: Run each stage in its own `try/catch` so you can identify which stage failed. Pass the output of each stage as input to the next. On failure, return immediately with the stage name and error message.
exercises.hint2: Three sequential try/catch blocks: `try { data = await pipeline.fetch(); } catch (err) { return { success: false, stage: "fetch", error: err.message }; }`. Same pattern for transform and validate. At the end return `{ success: true, data }`.
exercises.instructions: Write an async function that processes data through a pipeline of async stages (fetch, transform, validate), with error handling at each step.
hints: A data pipeline runs stages in sequence: fetch, transform, validate. Each stage can fail independently, so wrap each one in its own try/catch to identify which stage caused the failure.

Run each stage (`fetch`, `transform`, `validate`) in its own try/catch block, passing the output of one as input to the next. On failure, return immediately with the stage name and error message. If all stages complete, return the success result.

exercises.title: Recursive Product of Array
exercises.description: Create a function called `productOfArray` that accepts an array of numbers and returns the product of all numbers in the array using recursion. Do not use loops. The function should handle the base case of an empty array (returning 1) and multiply the first element by the recursive result of the remaining elements.
exercises.instructions:
Create a function called `productOfArray` that accepts an array of numbers and returns the product of all numbers using recursion.

Rules:
- Do not use any loops (`for`, `while`, `do...while`)
- Use recursion: the function must call itself
- An empty array should return `1` (the multiplicative identity)

Examples:
  productOfArray([1, 2, 3]) → 6
  productOfArray([1, 2, 3, 10]) → 60
  productOfArray([0, 5, 10]) → 0
  productOfArray([]) → 1
hints: Every recursive function needs a base case (when to stop) and a recursive case (when to call itself again). What should happen when the array is empty?
Multiply the first element `arr[0]` by the result of calling the function on the rest of the array. Use `arr.slice(1)` to get everything after the first element.

resources.label: MDN: Array.prototype.slice()
resources.description: Create a sub-array without modifying the original

exercises.title: Recursive Linear Search
exercises.description: Create a function called `recursiveSearch` that accepts an array and a target value. It should search the array for the target using recursion (no loops) and return the index where the target is found, or `-1` if not found. Use an optional parameter to track the current index.
exercises.instructions:
Create a function called `recursiveSearch` that accepts an array and a target value and returns the index of the target using recursion.

Rules:
- Do not use any loops
- Do not use `indexOf`, `findIndex`, or `includes`
- The function must call itself to check each element
- Return `-1` if the target is not in the array

Examples:
  recursiveSearch([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 3) → 2
  recursiveSearch([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 6) → -1
  recursiveSearch(["a", "b", "c"], "b") → 1
  recursiveSearch([], 1) → -1
exercises.starterCode:
/**
 * Search an array for a target value using recursion.
 * Return the index if found, or -1 if not found.
 *
 * @param {Array} arr - array to search
 * @param {*} target - value to find
 * @param {number} [idx=0] - current index (used in recursive calls)
 * @returns {number} index of target, or -1
 */
function recursiveSearch(arr, target, idx) {

}
hints: You need two base cases: one for when you have searched past the end of the array, and one for when you find a match at the current index.
Use a third parameter `idx` that starts at 0. If `arr[idx] === target`, return `idx`. If `idx >= arr.length`, return -1. Otherwise, call the function again with `idx + 1`.

exercises.title: Parallel Fetch All
exercises.description: Create a function called `fetchAll` that takes an array of async functions (each returns a Promise) and runs them all in parallel using `Promise.all`. Return an array of all resolved values. If any single promise rejects, the entire operation should reject with that error.
exercises.hint1: You need to call each function to get its Promise, then pass all Promises to a method that waits for all of them to complete simultaneously.
exercises.hint2: Map over the array to invoke each function, collecting the Promises. Then use a built-in Promise method that resolves when every Promise in the array resolves.
exercises.instructions: Create a function called `fetchAll` that takes an array of async functions (each returns a Promise) and runs them all in parallel using `Promise.all`. Return an array of all resolved values. If any single promise rejects, the entire operation should reject with that error.
hints: Promise.all runs an array of Promises in parallel and resolves when all of them complete. If any single Promise rejects, the whole result rejects.
You need to invoke each function in the array to get its Promise before passing them to `Promise.all`. Think about which array method lets you call each function and collect the results.

exercises.title: Race to Finish
exercises.description: Create a function called `raceToFinish` that takes an array of Promises and returns the value of whichever Promise settles first (resolves or rejects). If the first to settle is a rejection, the returned Promise should reject with that error.
exercises.hint1: There is a built-in Promise method that resolves or rejects as soon as the first Promise in the array settles. You just need to pass the array to it.
exercises.hint2: The method you need returns a Promise that adopts the state of the first Promise to settle — whether it resolves or rejects.
exercises.instructions: Create a function called `raceToFinish` that takes an array of Promises and returns the value of whichever Promise settles first (resolves or rejects). If the first to settle is a rejection, the returned Promise should reject with that error.
hints: There is a Promise combinator that settles as soon as the very first Promise in the array resolves or rejects. The result takes on that first settlement.
The input is already an array of Promises, so no invocation step is needed. Pass it directly to the appropriate combinator and return the result.

exercises.title: Collect All Outcomes
exercises.description: Create a function called `collectOutcomes` that takes an array of Promises and returns an array of result objects. Each result should be `{ status: "fulfilled", value: ... }` for resolved Promises or `{ status: "rejected", reason: ... }` for rejected Promises. Never reject — always return all outcomes.
exercises.hint1: There is a Promise method that waits for ALL Promises to settle (both resolve and reject) and returns an array of outcome objects. It never rejects itself.
exercises.hint2: The outcome objects from this method have `status`, `value` (for fulfilled), and `reason` (for rejected). You may need to extract `reason.message` if the reason is an Error object.
exercises.instructions: Create a function called `collectOutcomes` that takes an array of Promises and returns an array of result objects. Each result should be `{ status: "fulfilled", value: ... }` for resolved Promises or `{ status: "rejected", reason: ... }` for rejected Promises. Never reject — always return all outcomes.
hints: There is a Promise combinator that never rejects. It waits for every Promise to settle and returns an array of outcome objects describing each result.
Map over the settled results, normalizing each outcome into a consistent shape based on whether it fulfilled or rejected.

exercises.title: Async Find First
exercises.description: Create a function called `asyncFind` that takes an array of values and an async predicate function. It should test each value sequentially (one at a time, in order) using the predicate, and return the first value for which the predicate resolves to `true`. If no value passes, return `undefined`. Do not test remaining values after finding a match.
exercises.hint1: You cannot use `.find()` here because the predicate is async. Instead, loop through the values one at a time, awaiting the predicate for each, and return immediately when you find a match.
exercises.hint2: Use a `for` loop (not `.forEach` or `.map` — those do not support `await` correctly). Inside: `const result = await predicate(values[i]);` then check `if (result)` and return early.
exercises.instructions: Create a function called `asyncFind` that takes an array of values and an async predicate function. It should test each value sequentially (one at a time, in order) using the predicate, and return the first value for which the predicate resolves to `true`. If no value passes, return `undefined`. Do not test remaining values after finding a match.
hints: Standard array methods like `find` do not work with async predicates because they cannot await inside their callbacks. You need a loop construct that supports `await`.
Use a loop that supports await to test values one at a time. Return immediately on the first truthy result.

exercises.title: Aggregate Async Errors
exercises.description: Create a function called `aggregateErrors` that takes an array of async functions and runs them all in parallel. Return an object with `{ successes: [...values], errors: [...errorMessages] }`. Every function should be attempted regardless of failures — never short-circuit. Preserve the order of successes and errors relative to the original array.
exercises.hint1: You need a way to run all functions in parallel but NOT short-circuit on failure. There is a Promise combinator that waits for everything to settle regardless of outcome.
exercises.hint2: Map over the functions to invoke them (getting Promises), then use the combinator that collects all outcomes. Loop through the results and separate fulfilled values from rejected reasons.
exercises.instructions: Create a function called `aggregateErrors` that takes an array of async functions and runs them all in parallel. Return an object with `{ successes: [...values], errors: [...errorMessages] }`. Every function should be attempted regardless of failures — never short-circuit. Preserve the order of successes and errors relative to the original array.
hints: When you need to run multiple async operations in parallel without short-circuiting on failure, use a combinator that collects all outcomes regardless of whether each one resolves or rejects.
Invoke each function to get its Promise, then use the appropriate combinator. Iterate the settled outcomes and separate them into two arrays based on their status.

exercises.title: Parallel with Timeout
exercises.description: Create a function called `fetchWithTimeout` that takes an array of async functions and a timeout in milliseconds. Run all functions in parallel, but if the entire batch does not complete within the timeout, reject with an Error whose message is "Timeout after Nms" (where N is the timeout value). If all functions complete in time, return their resolved values as an array.
exercises.hint1: Create two competing Promises: one that resolves when all the async functions complete (parallel), and one that rejects after the timeout. Then race them against each other.
exercises.hint2: Use one combinator to run all functions in parallel (resolves when all complete). Create a timeout Promise with `setTimeout` that rejects with the error message. Then use another combinator that returns whichever settles first.
exercises.instructions: Create a function called `fetchWithTimeout` that takes an array of async functions and a timeout in milliseconds. Run all functions in parallel, but if the entire batch does not complete within the timeout, reject with an Error whose message is "Timeout after Nms" (where N is the timeout value). If all functions complete in time, return their resolved values as an array.
hints: The timeout pattern races the actual work against a timer. If the timer wins, the operation is considered failed. Two combinators work together here: one for parallel execution, one for racing.
Create two competing Promises: one representing all the parallel work completing, and one that rejects after the specified delay. Use the combinator that settles as soon as either one finishes.

exercises.title: Event Delegation
exercises.description: Create a function called `setupDelegatedList` that takes a `<ul>` element ID and sets up event delegation for click handling. Attach a single click event listener to the `<ul>` element (not to individual `<li>` items). When any `<li>` inside the list is clicked, toggle a CSS class called `"completed"` on that `<li>`. Clicks directly on the `<ul>` itself (not on an `<li>`) should do nothing. This pattern ensures that items added to the list later also respond to clicks without needing new listeners.
exercises.hint1: Instead of adding a click listener to each `<li>`, add one listener to the `<ul>`. Inside the handler, check `event.target` to see which element was actually clicked. Only act if the clicked element is an `<li>`.
exercises.hint2: Check `event.target.tagName` to determine if the clicked element is an `<li>`. If it is, use `classList.toggle()` to add or remove the class. Because the listener is on the parent, any new `<li>` elements will automatically trigger it.
exercises.instructions: Create a function called `setupDelegatedList` that takes a `<ul>` element ID and sets up event delegation for click handling. Attach a single click event listener to the `<ul>` element (not to individual `<li>` items). When any `<li>` inside the list is clicked, toggle a CSS class called `"completed"` on that `<li>`. Clicks directly on the `<ul>` itself (not on an `<li>`) should do nothing. This pattern ensures that items added to the list later also respond to clicks without needing new listeners.
hints: Event delegation attaches one listener to a parent element instead of individual children. The event object tells you which child was actually clicked.
Listen on the parent element and inspect `event.target` to determine which child triggered the event. Check the element's tag or class before acting on it.

exercises.title: Dynamic Sortable Table
exercises.description: Create a function called `buildSortableTable` that takes an array of objects and a container element ID. Build an HTML `<table>` inside the container with a `<thead>` row of `<th>` headers (from the object keys) and a `<tbody>` with one `<tr>` per object (one `<td>` per value). When a `<th>` header is clicked, sort the table rows by that column in ascending order. Clicking the same header again should toggle to descending order. The currently sorted header should display `" ▲"` (ascending) or `" ▼"` (descending) appended to the column name. Other headers should show just the column name with no indicator.
exercises.hint1: Build the table structure with `createElement` for `<table>`, `<thead>`, `<tbody>`, `<tr>`, `<th>`, and `<td>`. Add click listeners to each `<th>` that re-sort the data and rebuild the table body rows.
exercises.hint2: Keep track of the current sort column and direction in closure variables. When a header is clicked, check if it is the same column (toggle direction) or a new column (reset to ascending). Use `Array.sort()` with a comparison function, then clear and rebuild `<tbody>` rows.
exercises.instructions: Create a function called `buildSortableTable` that takes an array of objects and a container element ID. Build an HTML `<table>` inside the container with a `<thead>` row of `<th>` headers (from the object keys) and a `<tbody>` with one `<tr>` per object (one `<td>` per value). When a `<th>` header is clicked, sort the table rows by that column in ascending order. Clicking the same header again should toggle to descending order. The currently sorted header should display `" ▲"` (ascending) or `" ▼"` (descending) appended to the column name. Other headers should show just the column name with no indicator.
hints: A sortable table needs to track which column is currently sorted and in which direction. Clicking the same header toggles direction; clicking a different header resets to ascending.
Use closure variables to track sort state. On header click, re-sort the data array with a comparator, rebuild the table body, and update the header text to show the current sort indicator.

exercises.title: Tabs Component
exercises.description: Create a function called `createTabs` that takes an array of tab objects (each with `label` and `content` string properties) and a container element ID. Build a row of `<button>` elements with class `"tab-button"` (one per tab) and a set of `<div>` elements with class `"tab-panel"` (one per tab, containing the content text). The first tab should be active by default — its button gets an additional `"active"` class and its panel is visible. All other panels should have a `"hidden"` class. Clicking a tab button should show its panel (remove `"hidden"`), hide all other panels (add `"hidden"`), add `"active"` to the clicked button, and remove `"active"` from all other buttons.
exercises.hint1: Create buttons and panels in parallel arrays. Add a click listener to each button that loops through all buttons and panels — removing "active" from buttons and adding "hidden" to panels — then adds "active" to the clicked button and removes "hidden" from its matching panel.
exercises.hint2: Track buttons and panels in arrays indexed to match. In each click handler, loop through both arrays: `buttons[i].classList.remove("active")` and `panels[i].classList.add("hidden")`. Then toggle the current button and panel. The first tab starts as active and visible.
exercises.instructions: Create a function called `createTabs` that takes an array of tab objects (each with `label` and `content` string properties) and a container element ID. Build a row of `<button>` elements with class `"tab-button"` (one per tab) and a set of `<div>` elements with class `"tab-panel"` (one per tab, containing the content text). The first tab should be active by default — its button gets an additional `"active"` class and its panel is visible. All other panels should have a `"hidden"` class. Clicking a tab button should show its panel (remove `"hidden"`), hide all other panels (add `"hidden"`), add `"active"` to the clicked button, and remove `"active"` from all other buttons.
hints: A tab component shows one panel at a time. Each button is paired with a panel. Clicking a button should deactivate all tabs and activate only the clicked one.
Keep parallel arrays of buttons and panels. Each click handler needs to loop through all of them to reset state before activating the current pair.

exercises.title: Modal Dialog
exercises.description: Create a function called `setupModal` that takes a trigger button ID and a modal element ID. The modal element already exists in the DOM with a `"hidden"` class. When the trigger button is clicked, remove the `"hidden"` class from the modal and create an overlay `<div>` with class `"modal-overlay"` appended to `document.body`. The modal must contain an element with class `"modal-close"` — clicking it should add `"hidden"` back to the modal and remove the overlay from the DOM. Pressing the Escape key should also close the modal. Clicking the overlay itself should close the modal. If the modal is already hidden, Escape should do nothing.
exercises.hint1: Create open and close helper functions. The open function removes "hidden" from the modal and creates an overlay `<div>` appended to the body. The close function adds "hidden" back and removes the overlay. Wire up three ways to close: the close button, the Escape key, and clicking the overlay.
exercises.hint2: For Escape key handling, add a `"keydown"` listener to `document` that checks `event.key === "Escape"`. Only close if the modal is currently visible (does not have "hidden" class). For the overlay, create a new `<div>` each time the modal opens and remove it with `removeChild` when closing.
exercises.instructions: Create a function called `setupModal` that takes a trigger button ID and a modal element ID. The modal element already exists in the DOM with a `"hidden"` class. When the trigger button is clicked, remove the `"hidden"` class from the modal and create an overlay `<div>` with class `"modal-overlay"` appended to `document.body`. The modal must contain an element with class `"modal-close"` — clicking it should add `"hidden"` back to the modal and remove the overlay from the DOM. Pressing the Escape key should also close the modal. Clicking the overlay itself should close the modal. If the modal is already hidden, Escape should do nothing.
hints: A modal has multiple close triggers: a close button, the Escape key, and clicking the overlay background. The overlay is created dynamically when the modal opens and removed when it closes.

Write shared open/close helper functions. The open function shows the modal and creates an overlay. The close function hides the modal and removes the overlay. Wire all three close triggers to the same close function.

exercises.title: Accordion
exercises.description: Create a function called `createAccordion` that takes an array of section objects (each with `title` and `content` string properties) and a container element ID. Build an accordion where each section has a `<button>` with class `"accordion-header"` and a `<div>` with class `"accordion-content"`. All sections start collapsed (content has `"hidden"` class). Clicking a header should expand its content (remove `"hidden"`) and collapse all other sections (add `"hidden"` to their content). The expanded header should get an `"active"` class. Clicking an already-open header should collapse it (all sections closed). Only one section can be open at a time.
exercises.hint1: Track all headers and content panels in arrays. When any header is clicked, first close all sections (add "hidden" to all content, remove "active" from all headers). Then, if the clicked section was not already open, open it. This naturally enforces the one-at-a-time rule.
exercises.hint2: Before toggling, check if the current section is already open with `content.classList.contains("hidden")`. Loop through all sections to close them. Then, if the section was previously closed, remove "hidden" from its content and add "active" to its header.
exercises.instructions: Create a function called `createAccordion` that takes an array of section objects (each with `title` and `content` string properties) and a container element ID. Build an accordion where each section has a `<button>` with class `"accordion-header"` and a `<div>` with class `"accordion-content"`. All sections start collapsed (content has `"hidden"` class). Clicking a header should expand its content (remove `"hidden"`) and collapse all other sections (add `"hidden"` to their content). The expanded header should get an `"active"` class. Clicking an already-open header should collapse it (all sections closed). Only one section can be open at a time.
hints: An accordion allows only one section open at a time. The key interaction: clicking a header closes everything first, then opens the clicked section -- unless it was already open, in which case everything stays closed.
Track headers and content panels in paired arrays. On each click, check whether the clicked section is currently open before closing all sections. This determines whether to reopen the clicked one.

exercises.title: Live Form Validation
exercises.description: Create a function called `setupFormValidation` that takes a form element ID and a rules object. The rules object has field names as keys and rule objects as values. Each rule can have: `required` (boolean), `minLength` (number), and `maxLength` (number). For each field in the rules, find the `<input>` with that `name` attribute inside the form and attach an `"input"` event listener. On every keystroke, validate the current value against the rules. If validation fails, add a `"invalid"` class to the input and remove any `"valid"` class. If validation passes, add `"valid"` and remove `"invalid"`. Also create a `<span>` with class `"error-message"` immediately after each validated input — set its `textContent` to the first failing rule message or empty string if valid. Error messages should be: `"Required"` for empty required fields, `"Min N characters"` when too short, `"Max N characters"` when too long.
exercises.hint1: For each field in the rules object, find its input by `name` attribute, create an error `<span>` next to it, and add an `"input"` event listener. Inside the listener, check each rule in priority order (required, then minLength, then maxLength) and set the error message and CSS classes accordingly.
exercises.hint2: Use `form.querySelector('[name="fieldName"]')` to find each input. Insert the error span with `insertBefore(errorEl, input.nextSibling)`. In the input handler, check: if required and empty, show "Required"; else if too short, show "Min N characters"; else if too long, show "Max N characters"; else clear the error. Use `classList.add/remove` for "valid" and "invalid".
exercises.instructions: Create a function called `setupFormValidation` that takes a form element ID and a rules object. The rules object has field names as keys and rule objects as values. Each rule can have: `required` (boolean), `minLength` (number), and `maxLength` (number). For each field in the rules, find the `<input>` with that `name` attribute inside the form and attach an `"input"` event listener. On every keystroke, validate the current value against the rules. If validation fails, add a `"invalid"` class to the input and remove any `"valid"` class. If validation passes, add `"valid"` and remove `"invalid"`. Also create a `<span>` with class `"error-message"` immediately after each validated input — set its `textContent` to the first failing rule message or empty string if valid. Error messages should be: `"Required"` for empty required fields, `"Min N characters"` when too short, `"Max N characters"` when too long.
hints: Live form validation listens for input events on each field and checks the current value against a set of rules on every keystroke. An error span next to each input displays the first failing rule.

For each field in the rules object, find its input element, create an adjacent error span, and attach an `input` event listener. Inside the listener, check rules in priority order and toggle CSS classes based on validity.

exercises.title: Rethrow with Context
exercises.description: Create a function called `withContext` that takes a function `fn` and a string `context`. It should return a new function that calls `fn` with the same arguments. If `fn` executes successfully, return its result. If `fn` throws an error, catch it and throw a new `Error` whose message is `"[context] original message"` (the context string in square brackets followed by a space and the original error message). This wrapping pattern adds meaningful context to errors so you can trace where they originated.
exercises.hint1: Return a new function that wraps `fn` in a try/catch. In the catch block, create a new Error that combines the context string in brackets with the original error message, then throw it.
exercises.hint2: Use `fn.apply(null, arguments)` or the spread operator to forward all arguments to the original function. In the catch, build the message with string concatenation: `"[" + context + "] " + err.message`.
exercises.instructions: Create a function called `withContext` that takes a function `fn` and a string `context`. It should return a new function that calls `fn` with the same arguments. If `fn` executes successfully, return its result. If `fn` throws an error, catch it and throw a new `Error` whose message is `"[context] original message"` (the context string in square brackets followed by a space and the original error message). This wrapping pattern adds meaningful context to errors so you can trace where they originated.
hints: This is a higher-order function pattern: wrap another function in a try-catch and, on failure, throw a new Error that prepends context information to the original error message.
Return a new function that forwards all arguments to the original function. In the catch block, construct a new Error with the context string in brackets before the original message.

exercises.title: Error Collector
exercises.description: Create a function called `collectErrors` that takes an array of functions. Call each function (with no arguments) and collect the outcomes. Return an object with two arrays: `results` containing `{ index, value }` for each successful call, and `errors` containing `{ index, message }` for each function that threw. The `index` is the position of the function in the input array (starting at 0). Process every function — do not stop at the first error. The function itself should never throw.
exercises.hint1: Loop through the array with a `for` loop. Wrap each function call in its own try/catch so one failure does not stop the loop. Push successful values and caught errors into separate arrays, including the loop index with each entry.
exercises.hint2: For each index `i`, try calling `operations[i]()`. On success, push `{ index: i, value: result }` to the results array. On catch, push `{ index: i, message: err.message }` to the errors array. Return both arrays in an object.
exercises.instructions: Create a function called `collectErrors` that takes an array of functions. Call each function (with no arguments) and collect the outcomes. Return an object with two arrays: `results` containing `{ index, value }` for each successful call, and `errors` containing `{ index, message }` for each function that threw. The `index` is the position of the function in the input array (starting at 0). Process every function — do not stop at the first error. The function itself should never throw.
hints: Error collection means wrapping each function call in its own try-catch so that one failure does not stop the loop. Track both successes and failures with their position in the original array.
Iterate through the array with an indexed loop. For each function, try calling it and record the outcome (value or error message) along with the index into the appropriate output array.

exercises.title: Defensive Guard
exercises.description: Create a function called `processTransaction` that takes a transaction object and validates it thoroughly before processing. Check ALL of the following rules, collecting every error (not stopping at the first one): `type` must be a string equal to `"credit"` or `"debit"`; `amount` must be a number greater than 0; `account` must be a non-empty string; `timestamp` must be a number (Unix milliseconds). If there are validation errors, return `{ valid: false, errors: errors }` where `errors` is an array of strings describing each failure. If all checks pass, return `{ valid: true, processed: { type, amount, account, timestamp } }`. If the input is not an object or is null, return a single error: `"Transaction must be an object"`.
exercises.hint1: First check if the input is a valid object (not null, not an array, typeof is "object"). Then check each field one by one, pushing error strings into an array. At the end, if the array is empty all checks passed; otherwise return the collected errors.
exercises.hint2: Guard against non-objects first. Then build an errors array: check `typeof txn.type === "string"` and value is "credit" or "debit"; check `typeof txn.amount === "number"` and greater than 0; check `typeof txn.account === "string"` and trimmed is not empty; check `typeof txn.timestamp === "number"`. Return `{ valid: false, errors }` or `{ valid: true, processed: {...} }`.
exercises.instructions: Create a function called `processTransaction` that takes a transaction object and validates it thoroughly before processing. Check ALL of the following rules, collecting every error (not stopping at the first one): `type` must be a string equal to `"credit"` or `"debit"`; `amount` must be a number greater than 0; `account` must be a non-empty string; `timestamp` must be a number (Unix milliseconds). If there are validation errors, return `{ valid: false, errors: errors }` where `errors` is an array of strings describing each failure. If all checks pass, return `{ valid: true, processed: { type, amount, account, timestamp } }`. If the input is not an object or is null, return a single error: `"Transaction must be an object"`.
hints: Defensive programming validates every field independently and collects all errors before deciding whether the input is valid. Guard against non-object inputs first, then check each field separately.

First handle the null/non-object case as a special early return. Then check each field's type and value constraints, pushing a descriptive string into an errors array for each failure. Return based on whether the errors array is empty.

exercises.title: Error Pipeline
exercises.description: Create a function called `pipeline` that takes an array of data items and an array of transformation functions (steps). Each item should pass through every step in order. If a step throws for a particular item, that item is removed from processing and added to a `failed` array with details about the failure. Items that survive all steps go into a `passed` array. Return `{ passed: [...], failed: [...] }` where each `failed` entry is `{ item: originalItem, step: stepIndex, error: errorMessage }` (`step` is the 0-based index of the step that failed). Items that fail at an earlier step should not be processed by later steps.
exercises.hint1: For each step, loop through the current set of passing items. Wrap each step call in try/catch. If it succeeds, keep the transformed item. If it fails, move the item to the failed array with the step index and error message. Only surviving items continue to the next step.
exercises.hint2: Start with a copy of the data array. For each step index, create a new "surviving" array. Loop through current items: try applying the step function, push the result to surviving on success, or push `{ item, step, error }` to failed on catch. Replace the current items with the surviving array before moving to the next step.
exercises.instructions: Create a function called `pipeline` that takes an array of data items and an array of transformation functions (steps). Each item should pass through every step in order. If a step throws for a particular item, that item is removed from processing and added to a `failed` array with details about the failure. Items that survive all steps go into a `passed` array. Return `{ passed: [...], failed: [...] }` where each `failed` entry is `{ item: originalItem, step: stepIndex, error: errorMessage }` (`step` is the 0-based index of the step that failed). Items that fail at an earlier step should not be processed by later steps.
hints: A data pipeline passes each item through a series of transformation steps. If a step throws for a particular item, that item is removed from further processing and recorded as failed.

Use nested iteration: outer loop over steps, inner loop over surviving items. Apply each step inside a try-catch, keeping only items that succeed. Failed items get recorded with the step index and error message.

exercises.title: Validate Email Format
exercises.description: Create a function called `isValidEmail` that takes a string and returns `true` if it matches a basic email format, or `false` otherwise. A valid email has: one or more word characters or dots or hyphens before the `@`, then one or more word characters or hyphens after the `@`, then a dot, then two or more letters at the end. Use a regular expression with the `test` method.
exercises.hint1: A regular expression can validate the format. Use `^` and `$` to match the entire string. `\w` matches word characters (letters, digits, underscore). The `test` method returns true or false.
exercises.hint2: Build the pattern in parts: `^[\w.\-]+` for the local part, `@` literal, `[\w\-]+` for the domain, `\.` for the dot, `[a-zA-Z]{2,}$` for the TLD. Combine them and use `/pattern/.test(str)`.
exercises.instructions: Create a function called `isValidEmail` that takes a string and returns `true` if it matches a basic email format, or `false` otherwise. A valid email has: one or more word characters or dots or hyphens before the `@`, then one or more word characters or hyphens after the `@`, then a dot, then two or more letters at the end. Use a regular expression with the `test` method.
hints: A regular expression can validate email format by matching the structure: local part, at sign, domain, dot, and TLD. Anchor the pattern to the full string so partial matches fail.

Build the regex in sections for each part of the email. Use character classes for allowed characters in each section and a quantifier to enforce minimum TLD length. The `test` method returns a boolean.

exercises.title: Extract Numbers
exercises.description: Create a function called `extractNumbers` that takes a string and returns an array of all numbers found in it (as actual numbers, not strings). Numbers can be integers or decimals and can be negative. If no numbers are found, return an empty array. Use the `match` method with a global regex.
exercises.hint1: Use `String.match()` with a global regex (`/pattern/g`). The pattern needs to match optional negative sign, one or more digits, optional decimal point with more digits. Convert matches from strings to numbers.
exercises.hint2: The pattern `-?\d+\.?\d*` matches: optional minus, one-or-more digits, optional dot, zero-or-more digits. `str.match(/pattern/g)` returns an array of all matches (or `null` if none). Convert each match with `Number()` or `parseFloat()`.
exercises.instructions: Create a function called `extractNumbers` that takes a string and returns an array of all numbers found in it (as actual numbers, not strings). Numbers can be integers or decimals and can be negative. If no numbers are found, return an empty array. Use the `match` method with a global regex.
hints: Use `match` with a global regex to find all numbers in a string. The pattern needs to handle optional negative signs, integers, and decimals. Convert the string matches to actual numbers.
Use a global regex pattern that accounts for optional negative signs, integers, and decimals. Handle the case where no matches are found.

exercises.title: Count Word Occurrences
exercises.description: Create a function called `countWord` that takes a text string and a word string, then returns how many times that exact word appears in the text. The search should be case-insensitive and match whole words only (not substrings inside other words). For example, searching for `"the"` should not match `"there"` or `"other"`. Use a regular expression with word boundary anchors and appropriate flags.
exercises.hint1: You need a regex that matches the word with boundaries on each side and is case-insensitive. Since the word is a variable, use `new RegExp()` to build the pattern dynamically. Word boundaries prevent matching inside other words.
exercises.hint2: Build the regex with `new RegExp("\\b" + word + "\\b", "gi")`. The `\\b` is a word boundary anchor, `g` flag finds all matches, `i` flag makes it case-insensitive. Use `.match()` and check for null before reading `.length`.
exercises.instructions: Create a function called `countWord` that takes a text string and a word string, then returns how many times that exact word appears in the text. The search should be case-insensitive and match whole words only (not substrings inside other words). For example, searching for `"the"` should not match `"there"` or `"other"`. Use a regular expression with word boundary anchors and appropriate flags.
hints: Word boundary anchors in regex match the position between a word character and a non-word character, preventing partial word matches. Since the search word is a variable, construct the regex dynamically.
Construct the regex dynamically using word boundary anchors around the search term. Use flags for global and case-insensitive matching.

exercises.title: Format Phone Number
exercises.description: Create a function called `formatPhone` that takes a string containing a phone number in any common format and returns it formatted as `"(XXX) XXX-XXXX"`. First extract all digits from the input. If the result has exactly 10 digits, format them. If the result has 11 digits starting with `1` (country code), drop the leading `1` and format the remaining 10. For any other count of digits, return `null`.
exercises.hint1: First strip all non-digit characters from the string using `replace` with a regex that matches non-digits. Then check the digit count: 10 is ready to format, 11 starting with "1" means remove the first digit, anything else returns null.
exercises.hint2: Use `str.replace(/\D/g, "")` to get only digits. Check `.length` — if 11 and starts with "1", slice off the first character. If length is 10, build the output with string slicing: `"(" + digits.slice(0,3) + ") " + digits.slice(3,6) + "-" + digits.slice(6)`.
exercises.instructions: Create a function called `formatPhone` that takes a string containing a phone number in any common format and returns it formatted as `"(XXX) XXX-XXXX"`. First extract all digits from the input. If the result has exactly 10 digits, format them. If the result has 11 digits starting with `1` (country code), drop the leading `1` and format the remaining 10. For any other count of digits, return `null`.
hints: The approach is to strip all non-digit characters first, then check whether the resulting digit string has a valid length. Handle the US country code case (11 digits starting with 1) separately.
Use a regex replacement to extract only digits. Check the digit count and conditionally remove a leading country code. Then use string slicing to assemble the formatted output.

exercises.title: Capitalize Words
exercises.description: Create a function called `capitalizeWords` that takes a string and returns a new string with the first letter of every word capitalized and the rest lowercase. A word starts after a space or at the beginning of the string. Use `replace` with a regular expression. Handle multiple spaces between words and preserve them.
exercises.hint1: First convert the entire string to lowercase so you start with a clean base. Then use `replace` with a regex that matches the first letter of each word. The callback function receives each match and should return it uppercased.
exercises.hint2: The pattern `\b[a-z]` matches a lowercase letter at a word boundary (start of a word). With the `g` flag, it finds all such letters. Use `.replace(/\b[a-z]/g, function(match) { return match.toUpperCase(); })` on the lowercased string.
exercises.instructions: Create a function called `capitalizeWords` that takes a string and returns a new string with the first letter of every word capitalized and the rest lowercase. A word starts after a space or at the beginning of the string. Use `replace` with a regular expression. Handle multiple spaces between words and preserve them.
hints: To capitalize every word, first normalize the entire string to lowercase, then use a regex replacement to target the first letter of each word and convert it to uppercase.
Normalize the string to lowercase first, then use a regex replacement with a callback to uppercase the first letter of each word.

exercises.title: Parse Key-Value Pairs
exercises.description: Create a function called `parseKeyValue` that takes a string of key-value pairs and returns an object. Pairs are separated by semicolons (`;`). Each pair has the format `key=value`. Keys are one or more word characters. Values can be either unquoted (word characters only) or quoted with double quotes (which can contain any character except double quotes). Strip the quotes from quoted values. Ignore any extra whitespace around keys, values, and separators.
exercises.hint1: Split the string on semicolons to get individual pairs. For each pair, use a regex with capture groups to extract the key and value. The value might be quoted (surrounded by double quotes) or unquoted.
exercises.hint2: Split on ";", trim each piece, skip empty ones. Try matching against a quoted pattern first: `/(\w+)\s*=\s*"([^"]*)"` (key, then equals, then quoted value). If that fails, try unquoted: `/(\w+)\s*=\s*(\w*)` (key, then equals, then word chars). The captured groups give you key and value.
exercises.instructions: Create a function called `parseKeyValue` that takes a string of key-value pairs and returns an object. Pairs are separated by semicolons (`;`). Each pair has the format `key=value`. Keys are one or more word characters. Values can be either unquoted (word characters only) or quoted with double quotes (which can contain any character except double quotes). Strip the quotes from quoted values. Ignore any extra whitespace around keys, values, and separators.
hints: Split the input on the pair separator to get individual key-value strings, then parse each pair. Values can be either plain words or double-quoted strings that may contain spaces and special characters.
For each pair, try matching against a regex pattern for quoted values first, then fall back to an unquoted pattern. Use capture groups to extract the key and value separately.

exercises.title: Slug Generator
exercises.description: Create a function called `slugify` that converts a title string into a URL-friendly slug. The rules are: convert to lowercase, replace spaces and any non-alphanumeric characters with hyphens, collapse consecutive hyphens into a single hyphen, and remove leading and trailing hyphens. For example, `"Hello World!"` becomes `"hello-world"`.
exercises.hint1: Chain multiple string operations: lowercase first, then replace all non-alphanumeric characters with hyphens, then collapse runs of hyphens into one, and finally remove any hyphens at the start or end.
exercises.hint2: Use `.toLowerCase()` first. Then `.replace(/[^a-z0-9]+/g, "-")` to replace any sequence of non-alphanumeric characters with a single hyphen. Finally `.replace(/^-+|-+$/g, "")` to trim hyphens from the edges.
exercises.instructions: Create a function called `slugify` that converts a title string into a URL-friendly slug. The rules are: convert to lowercase, replace spaces and any non-alphanumeric characters with hyphens, collapse consecutive hyphens into a single hyphen, and remove leading and trailing hyphens. For example, `"Hello World!"` becomes `"hello-world"`.
hints: A URL slug is all lowercase, uses hyphens instead of spaces and special characters, has no consecutive hyphens, and no leading or trailing hyphens. Chain string operations to transform the input step by step.
Convert to lowercase first. Then replace runs of non-alphanumeric characters with a single hyphen. Finally, trim any hyphens from the start and end of the result.

exercises.title: Password Strength
exercises.description: Create a function called `checkPassword` that takes a string and returns an object describing its strength. Check these rules independently: `length` (at least 8 characters), `hasUpper` (contains at least one uppercase letter), `hasLower` (contains at least one lowercase letter), `hasDigit` (contains at least one digit), `hasSpecial` (contains at least one character that is not a letter or digit). Each property should be `true` or `false`. Also include a `score` property that counts how many of the five rules pass (0 to 5) and a `strong` property that is `true` only when all five rules pass.
exercises.hint1: Test each rule independently using a separate regex for each: uppercase `[A-Z]`, lowercase `[a-z]`, digit `\d`, special character `[^a-zA-Z0-9]`. Check length with `.length`. Count the passing rules for the score.
exercises.hint2: Use `.test(str)` for each regex check. For special characters, `[^a-zA-Z0-9]` matches anything that is NOT a letter or digit. Sum the boolean results (cast to 1 or 0) for the score. `strong` is true when score equals 5.
exercises.instructions: Create a function called `checkPassword` that takes a string and returns an object describing its strength. Check these rules independently: `length` (at least 8 characters), `hasUpper` (contains at least one uppercase letter), `hasLower` (contains at least one lowercase letter), `hasDigit` (contains at least one digit), `hasSpecial` (contains at least one character that is not a letter or digit). Each property should be `true` or `false`. Also include a `score` property that counts how many of the five rules pass (0 to 5) and a `strong` property that is `true` only when all five rules pass.
hints: Check each password rule independently using simple regex tests for character categories, plus a length check. Count how many rules pass to produce the score.
