Use separate regex patterns with `test()` for each character category: uppercase, lowercase, digit, and special character. Sum the boolean results and determine strength from the total.

exercises.title: Extract HTML Tags
exercises.description:
Create a function called `extractTags` that takes an HTML string and returns an array of unique tag names found in it, in order of first appearance. Extract tag names from opening tags like `
` and self-closing tags like `
`, but ignore closing tags like `
`. Tag names consist of letters and numbers. Ignore attributes inside tags — you only need the tag name. The result should contain each tag name only once, in lowercase.
exercises.hint1: Use a regex that matches opening tags: starts with `<`, then a letter followed by optional letters/digits (the tag name), then optional attributes, then `>` or `/>`. Use a capture group around the tag name. Loop with `exec` to find all matches.
exercises.hint2: The pattern `<([a-zA-Z][a-zA-Z0-9]*)` captures the tag name. Add `(?:\s[^>]*)?` to skip attributes, then `\/?>` to close. Use `regex.exec(html)` in a while loop with the `g` flag. Track seen tags in an object to ensure uniqueness.
exercises.instructions:
Create a function called `extractTags` that takes an HTML string and returns an array of unique tag names found in it, in order of first appearance. Extract tag names from opening tags like `
` and self-closing tags like `
`, but ignore closing tags like `
`. Tag names consist of letters and numbers. Ignore attributes inside tags — you only need the tag name. The result should contain each tag name only once, in lowercase.
hints: A regex can match opening HTML tags while ignoring closing tags. Use a capture group around the tag name to extract it. Loop through all matches while tracking which tags you have already seen.

Use `exec` in a while loop with the `g` flag to iterate through all matches. Convert each tag name to lowercase and use an object as a set to enforce uniqueness while preserving first-appearance order.

exercises.title: Template Engine
exercises.description: Create a function called `render` that takes a template string and a data object, and returns the template with all placeholders replaced. Placeholders use double curly braces: `{{key}}`. The function should support dot notation for nested values: `{{user.name}}` accesses `data.user.name`. If a placeholder references a key that does not exist, replace it with an empty string. Whitespace inside the braces should be trimmed: `{{ key }}` is the same as `{{key}}`.
exercises.hint1: Use `replace` with a regex that matches `{{...}}` and captures the key inside. In the replacement callback, split the key on dots and walk through the data object one level at a time. If any level is missing, return an empty string.
exercises.hint2: The regex `\{\{\s*([^}]+?)\s*\}\}` matches double braces with optional whitespace and captures the key. In the callback, split the key on `"."`, then loop: `value = value[parts[i]]`. Check for undefined/null at each step. Convert the final value to a string.
exercises.instructions: Create a function called `render` that takes a template string and a data object, and returns the template with all placeholders replaced. Placeholders use double curly braces: `{{key}}`. The function should support dot notation for nested values: `{{user.name}}` accesses `data.user.name`. If a placeholder references a key that does not exist, replace it with an empty string. Whitespace inside the braces should be trimmed: `{{ key }}` is the same as `{{key}}`.
hints: A template engine finds placeholders in the string and replaces each one with the corresponding value from a data object. Dot notation in the placeholder key means traversing nested properties.
Use `replace` with a regex that matches the placeholder syntax. In the callback, split the captured key on dots and walk through the data object one level at a time. Handle missing paths gracefully.

exercises.title: Flatten Nested Orders
exercises.description: Create a function called `flattenOrders` that takes an array of department objects. Each department has a `name` and a `regions` array. Each region has a `region` name and an `orders` array. Each order has `item` (string), `price` (number), and `qty` (number). Return an array of summary objects `{ department, orderCount, total }` where `total` is the sum of `price * qty` for all orders across all regions in that department. Sort the result by `total` descending.
exercises.hint1: For each department, you need to gather all orders from all regions into one flat array, then compute the total by summing `price * qty` for each order. Use `reduce` to concatenate region orders and to sum the totals.
exercises.hint2: Chain: `departments.map(dept => ...)` to build summaries. Inside, use `dept.regions.reduce((acc, r) => acc.concat(r.orders), [])` to flatten. Then `allOrders.reduce((sum, o) => sum + o.price * o.qty, 0)` for the total. Sort the mapped array by total descending.
exercises.instructions: Create a function called `flattenOrders` that takes an array of department objects. Each department has a `name` and a `regions` array. Each region has a `region` name and an `orders` array. Each order has `item` (string), `price` (number), and `qty` (number). Return an array of summary objects `{ department, orderCount, total }` where `total` is the sum of `price * qty` for all orders across all regions in that department. Sort the result by `total` descending.
hints: This is a flatten-then-aggregate pattern. For each top-level group, collect all nested items into a single array, compute an aggregate value from them, and sort the final summaries.

Iterate each department's regions to collect all orders into one flat array. Compute the total by summing the product of price and quantity for each order. Sort the final output by the computed total.

exercises.title: Student Grade Analysis
exercises.description: Create a function called `analyzeStudents` that takes an array of student objects. Each student has `name` (string), `grade` (string like `"A"`, `"B"`, etc.), and `courses` (array of `{ name, score }` objects). Group students by their `grade`. For each grade group, compute the average of all students' course averages (each student's average is the mean of their course scores). Return an array of `{ grade, count, avgScore }` objects sorted by `grade` alphabetically. Round `avgScore` to 2 decimal places.
exercises.hint1: First group students by grade into an object (keys are grades, values are arrays of students). Then for each group, compute each student's course average, then average those averages together. Sort the final array by grade.
exercises.hint2: Group with a `forEach` loop building an object. Then `Object.keys(groups).sort().map(...)` to process each grade. Each student's average is `courses.reduce((s, c) => s + c.score, 0) / courses.length`. The group average is the sum of student averages divided by the student count.
exercises.instructions: Create a function called `analyzeStudents` that takes an array of student objects. Each student has `name` (string), `grade` (string like `"A"`, `"B"`, etc.), and `courses` (array of `{ name, score }` objects). Group students by their `grade`. For each grade group, compute the average of all students' course averages (each student's average is the mean of their course scores). Return an array of `{ grade, count, avgScore }` objects sorted by `grade` alphabetically. Round `avgScore` to 2 decimal places.
hints: This is a two-level aggregation: first compute an average per student (from their courses), then average those student averages within each grade group. Group the data by grade before computing.

Build a grouping object keyed by grade. For each group, compute each student's course average, then average those averages across the group. Round the result and sort the output alphabetically by grade.

exercises.title: Deep Value Extraction
exercises.description: Create a function called `pluck` that takes an array of objects and a dot-notation path string. Extract the value at that path from each object. If the path does not exist in an object, use `undefined` for that entry. Return the array of extracted values. For example, `pluck([{ a: { b: 1 } }, { a: { b: 2 } }], "a.b")` returns `[1, 2]`.
exercises.hint1: Split the path on dots to get an array of keys. For each object, walk through the keys one by one, accessing deeper properties. If at any point the value is null or undefined, return undefined for that entry.
exercises.hint2: Use `arr.map(function(obj) { ... })` to process each item. Inside, start with `val = obj`, then loop through the path parts: `val = val[parts[i]]`. Check for null/undefined at each step. Return the final value.
exercises.instructions: Create a function called `pluck` that takes an array of objects and a dot-notation path string. Extract the value at that path from each object. If the path does not exist in an object, use `undefined` for that entry. Return the array of extracted values. For example, `pluck([{ a: { b: 1 } }, { a: { b: 2 } }], "a.b")` returns `[1, 2]`.
hints: Dot-notation path traversal means splitting a string like `a.b.c` into parts and walking through an object one key at a time. Handle cases where any intermediate level is missing.

For each object in the array, iterate through the path parts, accessing one level deeper at each step. If the current value becomes null or undefined at any point, stop and return undefined for that entry.

exercises.title: Transform Nested Tree
exercises.description: Create a function called `mapTree` that takes a tree node and a transform function. Each node is an object with a `value` property and an optional `children` array of child nodes. Apply the transform function to each node's `value` and return a new tree with the same structure but transformed values. The transform function takes `(value, depth)` where `depth` is 0 for the root. Do not mutate the original tree.
exercises.hint1: This requires recursion. Apply the transform to the current node's value, then recursively process each child. Track the depth by passing it as a parameter (starting at 0, incrementing for each level).
exercises.hint2: Create a new object with the transformed value. If the node has children, map over them with recursive calls: `node.children.map(child => mapTree(child, fn, depth + 1))`. If no children, just return the object without a children property.
exercises.instructions: Create a function called `mapTree` that takes a tree node and a transform function. Each node is an object with a `value` property and an optional `children` array of child nodes. Apply the transform function to each node's `value` and return a new tree with the same structure but transformed values. The transform function takes `(value, depth)` where `depth` is 0 for the root. Do not mutate the original tree.
hints: Recursive tree transformation applies a function to every node's value while preserving the tree structure. Track depth by incrementing a counter at each level of recursion.

Build a new node object with the transformed value. If the current node has children, recursively process each child. Return nodes without a children property when there are no children to preserve structure fidelity.

exercises.title: Cross-Reference Datasets
exercises.description: Create a function called `crossReference` that takes two arrays of objects, `primary` and `lookup`, and a `key` string. For each object in `primary`, find the matching object in `lookup` (where both have the same value for the given key). Merge the matching lookup properties into the primary object (lookup properties should not overwrite existing primary properties). If no match is found, add a `_matched` property set to `false`. If a match is found, add `_matched: true`. Return the merged array.
exercises.hint1: Build a lookup map from the secondary array (keyed by the join field) for O(1) access. Then map over the primary array, finding matches in the lookup. Merge properties from the match without overwriting existing properties.
exercises.hint2: Create the map: `lookup.forEach(item => map[item[key]] = item)`. For each primary item, copy its properties into a new object, then if a match exists, add any properties from the match that are not already present. Set `_matched` accordingly.
exercises.instructions: Create a function called `crossReference` that takes two arrays of objects, `primary` and `lookup`, and a `key` string. For each object in `primary`, find the matching object in `lookup` (where both have the same value for the given key). Merge the matching lookup properties into the primary object (lookup properties should not overwrite existing primary properties). If no match is found, add a `_matched` property set to `false`. If a match is found, add `_matched: true`. Return the merged array.
hints: Cross-referencing two datasets means matching records from one array to another by a shared key. Build an index from the lookup array for efficient matching, then merge properties without overwriting.

Index the lookup array into an object keyed by the join field. For each primary item, copy its properties into a new object, then add any properties from the matched lookup that do not already exist. Set a flag indicating whether a match was found.

exercises.title: Company Department Report
exercises.description: Create a function called `departmentReport` that takes a company object with structure: `{ departments: [{ name, teams: [{ name, members: [{ name, role, salary, active }] }] }] }`. Return an array of department summaries sorted by total salary descending. Each summary has: `department` (name), `teamCount` (number of teams), `activeMembers` (count of members where `active` is true across all teams), `totalSalary` (sum of all active members' salaries), and `topEarner` (name of the highest-paid active member, or `null` if no active members).
exercises.hint1: For each department, flatten all members from all teams, filter to active ones, then compute the sum of salaries and find the highest earner. Use `reduce` to find the top earner by comparing salaries.
exercises.hint2: Collect active members by looping through teams and their members, pushing active ones into an array. Use `reduce` for total salary and for finding the max. Handle the edge case where there are no active members (topEarner should be null).
exercises.instructions: Create a function called `departmentReport` that takes a company object with structure: `{ departments: [{ name, teams: [{ name, members: [{ name, role, salary, active }] }] }] }`. Return an array of department summaries sorted by total salary descending. Each summary has: `department` (name), `teamCount` (number of teams), `activeMembers` (count of members where `active` is true across all teams), `totalSalary` (sum of all active members' salaries), and `topEarner` (name of the highest-paid active member, or `null` if no active members).
hints: This requires traversing three levels of nesting: departments, teams, and members. For each department, flatten all members across teams, filter to active ones, then compute aggregates from the filtered set.

Collect active members per department by iterating teams and their members. Use the filtered list to compute salary totals, member counts, and find the highest earner. Handle the edge case of no active members.

exercises.title: Pivot Table
exercises.description: Create a function called `pivot` that takes an array of flat records, a `rowKey` (string), a `colKey` (string), and a `valueKey` (string). Reshape the data into a pivot table. Return an array of objects, one per unique `rowKey` value. Each object has a `_row` property (the row key value) plus one property for each unique `colKey` value (containing the sum of `valueKey` values for that row-column combination). If a row-column combination has no data, its value should be `0`. Sort rows alphabetically by `_row`.
exercises.hint1: First collect all unique column values. Then build a rows object where each key is a row value and each value is an object with the row name and all columns initialized to 0. Loop through records adding values to the correct row/column cell.
exercises.hint2: Two passes: (1) scan all records to find unique column values. (2) for each record, find or create the row object and add the value to the correct column. Finally, convert the rows object to an array, sorted by `_row`.
exercises.instructions: Create a function called `pivot` that takes an array of flat records, a `rowKey` (string), a `colKey` (string), and a `valueKey` (string). Reshape the data into a pivot table. Return an array of objects, one per unique `rowKey` value. Each object has a `_row` property (the row key value) plus one property for each unique `colKey` value (containing the sum of `valueKey` values for that row-column combination). If a row-column combination has no data, its value should be `0`. Sort rows alphabetically by `_row`.
hints: A pivot table reshapes flat records into a grid: one field becomes row headers, another becomes column headers, and a third is aggregated at each intersection. Missing combinations default to zero.

First collect all unique column values from the records. Build an accumulator object keyed by row values, initializing each column to zero. Iterate the records, adding each value to the correct row-column cell.

exercises.title: Inventory Analysis Pipeline
exercises.description: Create a function called `analyzeInventory` that takes an array of warehouse objects. Each warehouse has `name` (string), `location` (string), and `inventory` (array of `{ product, category, quantity, price }` objects). Perform this analysis pipeline: (1) Flatten all inventory items across all warehouses, tagging each with its warehouse name. (2) Filter out items with `quantity` of 0. (3) Compute the `totalValue` (`quantity * price`) for each item. (4) Group the remaining items by `category`. (5) For each category, return `{ category, itemCount, totalValue, topItem }` where `topItem` is the product name with the highest total value in that category. Sort the result by `totalValue` descending.
exercises.hint1: Build the pipeline step by step: flatten all inventory items (adding warehouse info), filter out zero-quantity items, compute total value for each, group by category, then summarize each group. Sort the final summaries by total value.
exercises.hint2: Flatten with nested forEach (or flatMap). Filter with `.filter(i => i.quantity > 0)`. Map to add `totalValue`. Group into an object by category. For each category, reduce to get the sum and the item with the highest individual value. Sort by totalValue descending.
exercises.instructions: Create a function called `analyzeInventory` that takes an array of warehouse objects. Each warehouse has `name` (string), `location` (string), and `inventory` (array of `{ product, category, quantity, price }` objects). Perform this analysis pipeline: (1) Flatten all inventory items across all warehouses, tagging each with its warehouse name. (2) Filter out items with `quantity` of 0. (3) Compute the `totalValue` (`quantity * price`) for each item. (4) Group the remaining items by `category`. (5) For each category, return `{ category, itemCount, totalValue, topItem }` where `topItem` is the product name with the highest total value in that category. Sort the result by `totalValue` descending.
hints: This is a multi-step data pipeline: flatten nested data, filter, compute derived values, group by category, then summarize each group. Process each step sequentially, passing the output of one step as input to the next.

Flatten inventory items across all sources, remove items that should be excluded, calculate a derived value for each remaining item, group them by a shared property, then aggregate each group into a summary with counts, totals, and a top item.

exercises.title: Stack Implementation
exercises.description: Create a `Stack` class that implements a Last-In-First-Out data structure. The constructor takes no arguments and initializes an empty stack. Implement these methods: `push(value)` adds a value to the top and returns the new size; `pop()` removes and returns the top value (returns `undefined` if empty); `peek()` returns the top value without removing it (returns `undefined` if empty); `size()` returns the number of items; `isEmpty()` returns `true` if the stack has no items; `toArray()` returns an array of all items from bottom to top.
exercises.hint1: Use an internal array to store items. `push` adds to the end, `pop` removes from the end, and `peek` reads the last element without removing it. This mirrors how a stack of plates works — you always add and remove from the top.
exercises.hint2: Store items in `this.items = []`. For `push`, use `this.items.push(value)` and return `this.items.length`. For `pop`, use `this.items.pop()`. For `peek`, return the element at index `this.items.length - 1`. For `toArray`, return a copy with `this.items.slice()`.
exercises.instructions: Create a `Stack` class that implements a Last-In-First-Out data structure. The constructor takes no arguments and initializes an empty stack. Implement these methods: `push(value)` adds a value to the top and returns the new size; `pop()` removes and returns the top value (returns `undefined` if empty); `peek()` returns the top value without removing it (returns `undefined` if empty); `size()` returns the number of items; `isEmpty()` returns `true` if the stack has no items; `toArray()` returns an array of all items from bottom to top.
hints: A stack follows Last-In-First-Out ordering, like a stack of plates. The most recently added item is always the first one removed. Consider which built-in array operations naturally behave this way.

Back the stack with an internal array. The key insight is that one end of the array serves as the "top" of the stack for all operations. Remember that `toArray` should return a copy, not the internal array itself.

exercises.title: Queue Implementation
exercises.description: Create a `Queue` class that implements a First-In-First-Out data structure. The constructor takes no arguments and initializes an empty queue. Implement these methods: `enqueue(value)` adds a value to the back and returns the new size; `dequeue()` removes and returns the front value (returns `undefined` if empty); `front()` returns the front value without removing it (returns `undefined` if empty); `size()` returns the number of items; `isEmpty()` returns `true` if the queue has no items; `toArray()` returns an array of all items from front to back.
exercises.hint1: Use an internal array where items enter from one end and leave from the other. Think of a line at a store — the first person in line is the first to be served. Add to the back, remove from the front.
exercises.hint2: Store items in `this.items = []`. For `enqueue`, use `this.items.push(value)` and return the new length. For `dequeue`, use `this.items.shift()` to remove from the front. For `front`, return `this.items[0]`. For `toArray`, return a copy with `this.items.slice()`.
exercises.instructions: Create a `Queue` class that implements a First-In-First-Out data structure. The constructor takes no arguments and initializes an empty queue. Implement these methods: `enqueue(value)` adds a value to the back and returns the new size; `dequeue()` removes and returns the front value (returns `undefined` if empty); `front()` returns the front value without removing it (returns `undefined` if empty); `size()` returns the number of items; `isEmpty()` returns `true` if the queue has no items; `toArray()` returns an array of all items from front to back.
hints: A queue follows First-In-First-Out ordering, like a line at a store. Items enter at one end and leave from the other. Think about which end of an array is efficient for adding and which for removing.

Use an internal array where you add to one end and remove from the other. Consider which array methods add to the back versus remove from the front. Handle the empty-queue case for both `dequeue` and `front`.

exercises.title: Linked List
exercises.description: Create a `LinkedList` class that implements a singly linked list. Each node should have a `value` and a `next` pointer. The constructor initializes an empty list with a `head` of `null`. Implement these methods: `append(value)` adds a node to the end; `prepend(value)` adds a node to the beginning; `size()` returns the number of nodes; `toArray()` returns an array of all values from head to tail; `find(value)` returns the first node with that value or `null` if not found; `removeAt(index)` removes the node at the given 0-based index and returns its value (returns `undefined` if index is out of bounds). You may define a separate `Node` class or use plain objects for nodes.
exercises.hint1: Each node is an object with `value` and `next` (pointing to the next node or null). To traverse, start at `this.head` and follow `.next` until you reach null. Append walks to the end, prepend replaces the head.
exercises.hint2: For `append`, create a node and if `this.head` is null, set it as head. Otherwise, walk to the last node (where `.next` is null) and set `.next` to the new node. For `removeAt`, handle index 0 specially by updating `this.head`. For other indices, walk to the node before the target and set its `.next` to skip the target node.
exercises.instructions: Create a `LinkedList` class that implements a singly linked list. Each node should have a `value` and a `next` pointer. The constructor initializes an empty list with a `head` of `null`. Implement these methods: `append(value)` adds a node to the end; `prepend(value)` adds a node to the beginning; `size()` returns the number of nodes; `toArray()` returns an array of all values from head to tail; `find(value)` returns the first node with that value or `null` if not found; `removeAt(index)` removes the node at the given 0-based index and returns its value (returns `undefined` if index is out of bounds). You may define a separate `Node` class or use plain objects for nodes.
hints: A linked list is a chain of nodes where each node holds a value and a reference to the next node. Unlike arrays, you cannot jump to a position by index -- you must traverse the chain from the head.
Traverse the chain from the head using a while loop. For removal, update the previous node's pointer to skip over the target node.

exercises.title: HashMap Implementation
exercises.description: Create a `HashMap` class that stores key-value pairs using a hash function and handles collisions with chaining (arrays at each bucket). The constructor takes an optional `size` parameter (default 16) for the number of buckets. Implement a `_hash(key)` method that converts a string key into a bucket index. Implement these methods: `set(key, value)` stores a key-value pair (update if key exists); `get(key)` returns the value for a key or `undefined` if not found; `has(key)` returns `true` if the key exists; `delete(key)` removes a key-value pair and returns `true` if it existed, `false` otherwise; `keys()` returns an array of all keys; `values()` returns an array of all values.
exercises.hint1: Create an array of buckets (arrays). Use a hash function that converts each character of the key into a number and mods by the bucket count. Each bucket stores `[key, value]` pairs. When two keys hash to the same bucket, they both go in that bucket's array — this is called chaining.
exercises.hint2: Initialize `this.buckets` as an array of empty arrays. For `_hash`, sum each `key.charCodeAt(i)` multiplied by position and mod by bucket size. For `set`, hash the key, then search that bucket for an existing entry with the same key — update it or push a new `[key, value]` pair. For `get`, hash and search the bucket for the matching key.
exercises.instructions: Create a `HashMap` class that stores key-value pairs using a hash function and handles collisions with chaining (arrays at each bucket). The constructor takes an optional `size` parameter (default 16) for the number of buckets. Implement a `_hash(key)` method that converts a string key into a bucket index. Implement these methods: `set(key, value)` stores a key-value pair (update if key exists); `get(key)` returns the value for a key or `undefined` if not found; `has(key)` returns `true` if the key exists; `delete(key)` removes a key-value pair and returns `true` if it existed, `false` otherwise; `keys()` returns an array of all keys; `values()` returns an array of all values.
hints: A hash map converts keys to array indices using a hash function, then stores entries at those indices. When two keys hash to the same index (a collision), you need a strategy to store both -- chaining uses a nested array at each bucket.

Build a hash function using character codes and modular arithmetic. Each bucket holds an array of `[key, value]` pairs. When setting a key, check the bucket for an existing entry with that key before adding a new one. When deleting, remove the matching pair from the bucket.

exercises.title: Binary Search Tree
exercises.description: Create a `BST` class that implements a binary search tree. Each node has a `value`, `left`, and `right` property. The constructor initializes the tree with a `root` of `null`. Implement these methods: `insert(value)` adds a value to the correct position (left if less than, right if greater than or equal to the current node); `contains(value)` returns `true` if the value exists in the tree; `min()` returns the smallest value (or `null` for empty tree); `max()` returns the largest value (or `null` for empty tree); `inOrder()` returns an array of values using in-order traversal (left, root, right — produces sorted output); `count()` returns the total number of nodes.
exercises.hint1: A BST organizes values so that everything less than a node goes left, everything greater goes right. To insert, start at the root and walk left or right until you find an empty spot. For in-order traversal, recursively visit left, then current, then right — this produces sorted output.
exercises.hint2: For `insert`, create a node object and if root is null, set it as root. Otherwise, loop: compare value to current node, go left if smaller, right if larger, and insert when you reach a null spot. For `inOrder`, use a recursive helper: call itself on `node.left`, push `node.value`, then call itself on `node.right`.
exercises.instructions: Create a `BST` class that implements a binary search tree. Each node has a `value`, `left`, and `right` property. The constructor initializes the tree with a `root` of `null`. Implement these methods: `insert(value)` adds a value to the correct position (left if less than, right if greater than or equal to the current node); `contains(value)` returns `true` if the value exists in the tree; `min()` returns the smallest value (or `null` for empty tree); `max()` returns the largest value (or `null` for empty tree); `inOrder()` returns an array of values using in-order traversal (left, root, right — produces sorted output); `count()` returns the total number of nodes.
hints: A binary search tree organizes values so that smaller values go left and larger values go right. This property makes searching efficient -- at each node you can eliminate half the remaining tree. In-order traversal visits left, node, right and produces sorted output.
Walk the tree comparing values to choose left or right. For traversal and counting, use recursive helpers with a null base case.

exercises.title: Graph with Traversal
exercises.description: Create a `Graph` class that implements an undirected graph using an adjacency list. The constructor initializes an empty graph. Implement these methods: `addVertex(vertex)` adds a vertex (does nothing if it already exists); `addEdge(v1, v2)` adds an undirected edge between two vertices (does nothing if the edge already exists or vertices do not exist); `getNeighbors(vertex)` returns an array of adjacent vertices (or empty array if vertex does not exist); `hasVertex(vertex)` returns `true` if the vertex exists; `hasEdge(v1, v2)` returns `true` if an edge exists between the two vertices; `bfs(start)` performs breadth-first search from the start vertex and returns an array of vertices in the order visited (returns empty array if start does not exist); `dfs(start)` performs depth-first search from the start vertex and returns an array of vertices in the order visited (returns empty array if start does not exist).
exercises.hint1: Store the graph as an object where each key is a vertex and each value is an array of neighbor vertices. For BFS, use a queue (process first-in, first-out) with a visited set. For DFS, use recursion or a stack (process last-in, first-out) with a visited set.
exercises.hint2: Use `this.adjacencyList = {}` where each key maps to an array of neighbors. For `addEdge`, push v2 into v1's array and v1 into v2's array (undirected). For BFS, start with the start vertex in a queue, mark it visited, then loop: shift from queue, push to result, add unvisited neighbors to queue. For DFS, use a recursive function that marks the vertex visited, pushes to result, then recurses on unvisited neighbors.
exercises.instructions: Create a `Graph` class that implements an undirected graph using an adjacency list. The constructor initializes an empty graph. Implement these methods: `addVertex(vertex)` adds a vertex (does nothing if it already exists); `addEdge(v1, v2)` adds an undirected edge between two vertices (does nothing if the edge already exists or vertices do not exist); `getNeighbors(vertex)` returns an array of adjacent vertices (or empty array if vertex does not exist); `hasVertex(vertex)` returns `true` if the vertex exists; `hasEdge(v1, v2)` returns `true` if an edge exists between the two vertices; `bfs(start)` performs breadth-first search from the start vertex and returns an array of vertices in the order visited (returns empty array if start does not exist); `dfs(start)` performs depth-first search from the start vertex and returns an array of vertices in the order visited (returns empty array if start does not exist).
hints: An adjacency list graph stores each vertex as a key with its neighbors as an array. For undirected edges, the connection must be recorded in both directions. BFS and DFS both need to track visited vertices to avoid infinite loops in cyclic graphs.

Store the graph as an object mapping vertex names to neighbor arrays. BFS processes vertices level by level using a queue. DFS goes deep before backtracking using recursion or a stack. Both should mark vertices as visited before processing their neighbors.

exercises.title: Binary Search
exercises.description: Create a function called `binarySearch` that takes a sorted array of numbers and a target value. It should find the target by repeatedly dividing the search space in half. Return the index of the target if found, or `-1` if the target is not in the array. Start with two pointers at the beginning and end of the array. Calculate the middle index, then compare the middle element to the target: if it matches, return the index; if the target is smaller, search the left half; if the target is larger, search the right half. Continue until the pointers cross.
exercises.hint1: Use two variables to track the current search boundaries — one for the left end and one for the right end. On each iteration, look at the element in the middle. If it matches, you are done. If the target is smaller, move the right boundary to just before the middle. If larger, move the left boundary to just after the middle.
exercises.hint2: Initialize `left = 0` and `right = arr.length - 1`. Loop while `left <= right`. Compute `mid = Math.floor((left + right) / 2)`. If `arr[mid] === target`, return `mid`. If `target < arr[mid]`, set `right = mid - 1`. Otherwise set `left = mid + 1`. If the loop ends without finding, return -1.
exercises.instructions: Create a function called `binarySearch` that takes a sorted array of numbers and a target value. It should find the target by repeatedly dividing the search space in half. Return the index of the target if found, or `-1` if the target is not in the array. Start with two pointers at the beginning and end of the array. Calculate the middle index, then compare the middle element to the target: if it matches, return the index; if the target is smaller, search the left half; if the target is larger, search the right half. Continue until the pointers cross.
hints: Binary search eliminates half the remaining candidates with each comparison. It requires a sorted array and uses two boundary pointers that narrow the search space. Think about what happens when the boundaries cross.

Maintain a left and right pointer. Compute the midpoint, compare with the target, and adjust the appropriate boundary. The loop condition and how you adjust boundaries after each comparison are the critical details.

exercises.title: Bubble Sort
exercises.description: Create a function called `bubbleSort` that takes an array of numbers and returns a new sorted array in ascending order. Bubble sort works by repeatedly stepping through the array, comparing adjacent elements, and swapping them if they are in the wrong order. After each full pass, the largest unsorted element "bubbles" to its correct position. Include an optimization: if a complete pass makes no swaps, the array is already sorted and you can stop early. Do not modify the original array.
exercises.hint1: Make a copy of the input array first. Use two nested loops — the outer loop tracks how many passes you have made, and the inner loop compares each pair of adjacent elements. If the left element is larger than the right, swap them. Track whether any swap occurred during a pass to enable early exit.
exercises.hint2: Copy with `arr.slice()`. Outer loop runs `n - 1` times. Inner loop runs from `0` to `n - 1 - i` (each pass puts one more element in place). Swap with a temp variable when `result[j] > result[j + 1]`. Set a `swapped` flag; if it is still `false` after a full inner pass, break out of the outer loop.
exercises.instructions: Create a function called `bubbleSort` that takes an array of numbers and returns a new sorted array in ascending order. Bubble sort works by repeatedly stepping through the array, comparing adjacent elements, and swapping them if they are in the wrong order. After each full pass, the largest unsorted element "bubbles" to its correct position. Include an optimization: if a complete pass makes no swaps, the array is already sorted and you can stop early. Do not modify the original array.
hints: Bubble sort repeatedly walks through the array comparing adjacent pairs and swapping them if they are out of order. After each full pass, one more element settles into its final position. An early-exit optimization can detect when the array is already sorted.

Copy the array first so you do not modify the original. Use nested loops -- the inner loop shrinks each pass since the end is already sorted. Track whether any swaps occurred during a pass to enable early termination.

exercises.title: Insertion Sort
exercises.description: Create a function called `insertionSort` that takes an array of numbers and returns a new sorted array in ascending order. Insertion sort works by building a sorted portion one element at a time. Start from the second element and compare it backward against the sorted portion. Shift larger elements to the right to make room, then insert the current element in its correct position. Do not modify the original array.
exercises.hint1: Think of it like sorting a hand of playing cards. You pick up one card at a time and insert it into the correct position among the cards you have already sorted. Start from index 1, save the current value, then shift elements to the right until you find the insertion point.
exercises.hint2: Copy the array first. Loop from index 1 to the end. Save `result[i]` as `current`. Use a while loop going backward: while `j >= 0` and `result[j] > current`, shift `result[j]` right by setting `result[j + 1] = result[j]` and decrementing `j`. After the while loop, place `current` at `result[j + 1]`.
exercises.instructions: Create a function called `insertionSort` that takes an array of numbers and returns a new sorted array in ascending order. Insertion sort works by building a sorted portion one element at a time. Start from the second element and compare it backward against the sorted portion. Shift larger elements to the right to make room, then insert the current element in its correct position. Do not modify the original array.
hints: Insertion sort builds a sorted portion one element at a time. Pick the next unsorted element and slide it into its correct position among the already-sorted elements by shifting larger elements to the right.

Copy the array first. Starting from the second element, save the current value, then use a backward loop to shift larger elements right until you find the insertion point. Place the saved value in the gap.

exercises.title: Merge Sort
exercises.description: Create a function called `mergeSort` that takes an array of numbers and returns a new sorted array in ascending order using the merge sort algorithm. Merge sort works by recursively splitting the array in half until each piece has one element, then merging the pieces back together in sorted order. Write a helper function that merges two sorted arrays into one sorted array by comparing their elements one at a time. The base case is an array with 0 or 1 elements (already sorted). Do not modify the original array.
exercises.hint1: Split the problem into two parts: a recursive function that divides the array in half until the pieces are trivially small, and a merge helper that combines two already-sorted arrays into one sorted array. The merge helper uses two index pointers that advance through each input array.
exercises.hint2: Base case: if `arr.length <= 1`, return a copy. Otherwise, split at the midpoint with `arr.slice(0, mid)` and `arr.slice(mid)`, recursively sort each half, then merge. The merge function uses pointers `i` and `j` — compare `a[i]` and `b[j]`, push the smaller one, advance that pointer. After one array is exhausted, append the remainder of the other.
exercises.instructions: Create a function called `mergeSort` that takes an array of numbers and returns a new sorted array in ascending order using the merge sort algorithm. Merge sort works by recursively splitting the array in half until each piece has one element, then merging the pieces back together in sorted order. Write a helper function that merges two sorted arrays into one sorted array by comparing their elements one at a time. The base case is an array with 0 or 1 elements (already sorted). Do not modify the original array.
hints: Merge sort splits the array in half recursively until each piece is trivially sorted (length 0 or 1), then merges the pieces back together in order. The merge step is the key operation -- combining two sorted arrays into one sorted array.

Write a merge helper with two index pointers that advance through two sorted arrays, always picking the smaller element. The main function splits at the midpoint, recurses on both halves, and merges the results. The base case returns a copy of arrays with 0 or 1 elements.

exercises.title: Quick Sort
exercises.description: Create a function called `quickSort` that takes an array of numbers and returns a new sorted array in ascending order using the quicksort algorithm. Pick the first element as the pivot. Partition the remaining elements into two groups: those less than the pivot and those greater than or equal to the pivot. Recursively sort each group, then combine: sorted-less, pivot, sorted-greater. The base case is an array with 0 or 1 elements. Do not modify the original array.
exercises.hint1: Choose the first element as your pivot. Loop through the remaining elements and put each one into either a "less than pivot" group or a "greater than or equal to pivot" group. Recursively sort both groups, then concatenate: sorted-less + pivot + sorted-greater.
exercises.hint2: Base case: if `arr.length <= 1`, return a copy. Set `pivot = arr[0]`. Loop from index 1 to end, pushing elements less than pivot into a `less` array and the rest into a `greater` array. Return `quickSort(less).concat([pivot], quickSort(greater))`.
exercises.instructions: Create a function called `quickSort` that takes an array of numbers and returns a new sorted array in ascending order using the quicksort algorithm. Pick the first element as the pivot. Partition the remaining elements into two groups: those less than the pivot and those greater than or equal to the pivot. Recursively sort each group, then combine: sorted-less, pivot, sorted-greater. The base case is an array with 0 or 1 elements. Do not modify the original array.
hints: Quicksort picks a pivot element and partitions the remaining elements into two groups -- those less than the pivot and those greater than or equal to it. Each group is recursively sorted, then the results are concatenated around the pivot.

Use the first element as the pivot. Loop through the rest of the array, partitioning into two groups. Recursively sort each group and concatenate: sorted-less, pivot, sorted-greater. The base case handles arrays of length 0 or 1.

exercises.title: Frequency Counter
exercises.description: Create a function called `findPairSum` that takes an array of numbers and a target sum. Return the first pair of numbers (as a two-element array `[a, b]`) where `a + b` equals the target, or `null` if no pair exists. Use the frequency counter (hash map) pattern: as you iterate through the array, store each number you have seen. For each new number, check if the complement (target minus current number) has already been seen. This approach finds the pair in a single pass through the array. Return the pair in the order they appear (the complement first, then the current number).
exercises.hint1: Instead of using nested loops to check every pair, use an object as a lookup table. For each number, calculate what value you would need to reach the target sum. If that needed value is already in your lookup table, you have found your pair. Otherwise, add the current number to the table and continue.
exercises.hint2: Create a `seen` object. Loop through the array. For each element, compute `complement = target - arr[i]`. Check if `seen[complement]` exists — if so, return `[complement, arr[i]]`. If not, set `seen[arr[i]] = true` and continue. Return `null` after the loop if no pair was found.
exercises.instructions: Create a function called `findPairSum` that takes an array of numbers and a target sum. Return the first pair of numbers (as a two-element array `[a, b]`) where `a + b` equals the target, or `null` if no pair exists. Use the frequency counter (hash map) pattern: as you iterate through the array, store each number you have seen. For each new number, check if the complement (target minus current number) has already been seen. This approach finds the pair in a single pass through the array. Return the pair in the order they appear (the complement first, then the current number).
hints: The frequency counter pattern uses an object as a lookup table to avoid nested loops. As you scan through data, you can instantly check whether a complementary value has already been seen, reducing a quadratic problem to linear time.

For each element, calculate what other value would complete the pair. Check your lookup object for that complement -- if found, you have your answer. Otherwise, record the current element and continue. Think about what to return when no pair is found.

exercises.title: Two Pointer Technique
exercises.description: Create a function called `threeSum` that takes a sorted array of numbers and a target sum. Find all unique triplets `[a, b, c]` where `a + b + c` equals the target. Return an array of triplets (each triplet is a three-element array). There should be no duplicate triplets in the result. Use the two-pointer technique: for each element, set a left pointer just after it and a right pointer at the end, then move them inward based on whether the current sum is too small or too large. Skip duplicate values to avoid duplicate triplets.
exercises.hint1: Fix one element at a time, then use two pointers on the remaining subarray to find pairs that complete the target sum. Since the array is sorted, if the current sum is too small move the left pointer right (to increase the sum), if too large move the right pointer left (to decrease it). Skip over duplicate values to avoid duplicate triplets.
exercises.hint2: Loop `i` from 0 to `arr.length - 2`. Skip if `arr[i] === arr[i-1]` (avoid duplicate first elements). Set `left = i + 1` and `right = arr.length - 1`. While `left < right`: compute sum. If equal to target, push the triplet and skip duplicates by advancing both pointers past repeated values. If sum is too small, increment left. If too large, decrement right.
exercises.instructions: Create a function called `threeSum` that takes a sorted array of numbers and a target sum. Find all unique triplets `[a, b, c]` where `a + b + c` equals the target. Return an array of triplets (each triplet is a three-element array). There should be no duplicate triplets in the result. Use the two-pointer technique: for each element, set a left pointer just after it and a right pointer at the end, then move them inward based on whether the current sum is too small or too large. Skip duplicate values to avoid duplicate triplets.
hints: The two-pointer technique works on sorted arrays by using a left and right pointer that move inward based on the current sum. For three-sum, fix one element and use two pointers on the remaining subarray. Skip duplicate values to avoid duplicate triplets.

The outer loop fixes one element while skipping duplicates. The inner two pointers adjust based on whether the three-element sum is too small (move left pointer right) or too large (move right pointer left). When a match is found, advance both pointers past any duplicate values.

exercises.title: Sliding Window
exercises.description: Create a function called `maxSubarraySum` that takes an array of numbers and a positive integer `k`. Find the maximum sum of any contiguous subarray of exactly `k` elements. Return the maximum sum, or `null` if the array has fewer than `k` elements. Use the sliding window technique: calculate the sum of the first `k` elements, then slide the window one position at a time by adding the next element and removing the element that fell off the left side. Track the maximum sum seen.
exercises.hint1: Instead of recalculating the sum of every subarray from scratch, compute the first window's sum, then "slide" the window forward: add the new element entering the window and subtract the element leaving. This turns a nested-loop problem into a single-pass solution. Track the maximum sum as you slide.
exercises.hint2: First check if `arr.length < k` and return null. Compute the initial window sum by looping from 0 to k-1. Set `maxSum = windowSum`. Then loop from `i = k` to end: update `windowSum = windowSum + arr[i] - arr[i - k]` and update `maxSum` if the new sum is larger. Return `maxSum`.
exercises.instructions: Create a function called `maxSubarraySum` that takes an array of numbers and a positive integer `k`. Find the maximum sum of any contiguous subarray of exactly `k` elements. Return the maximum sum, or `null` if the array has fewer than `k` elements. Use the sliding window technique: calculate the sum of the first `k` elements, then slide the window one position at a time by adding the next element and removing the element that fell off the left side. Track the maximum sum seen.
hints: The sliding window technique avoids recalculating the sum of every subarray from scratch. Instead, maintain a running sum and update it incrementally as the window moves -- one element enters, one element leaves.

Compute the initial window sum, then slide forward by adding the entering element and subtracting the departing element. Track the maximum sum seen. Handle the edge case where the array is shorter than the window size.

exercises.title: Singleton Pattern
exercises.description: Create a function called `createConfigManager` that returns a config manager object. The manager must be a singleton — every call to `createConfigManager()` must return the exact same object reference. The manager has these methods: `get(key)` returns the value for a key or `undefined` if not set; `set(key, value)` stores a key-value pair; `getAll()` returns a shallow copy of all stored config as a plain object; `reset()` clears all stored config. Use a closure to store the single instance and the config data privately.
exercises.hint1: Wrap the entire function in an IIFE (Immediately Invoked Function Expression) that keeps a private `instance` variable. Each time the outer function is called, check if `instance` already exists — if so, return it. If not, create the manager object, store it in `instance`, and return it.
exercises.hint2: Use the pattern `var createConfigManager = (function() { var instance = null; var config = {}; return function() { if (instance) return instance; instance = { get, set, getAll, reset }; return instance; }; })();`. The closure ensures `instance` and `config` are private and shared across all calls.
exercises.instructions: Create a function called `createConfigManager` that returns a config manager object. The manager must be a singleton — every call to `createConfigManager()` must return the exact same object reference. The manager has these methods: `get(key)` returns the value for a key or `undefined` if not set; `set(key, value)` stores a key-value pair; `getAll()` returns a shallow copy of all stored config as a plain object; `reset()` clears all stored config. Use a closure to store the single instance and the config data privately.
hints: The singleton pattern ensures only one instance of an object ever exists by using a closure to store the instance privately. The first call creates it; subsequent calls return the saved reference. The internal data should also be inaccessible from outside.

Wrap the factory function in an IIFE that captures a private `instance` variable. The returned function checks whether the instance already exists before creating a new one. Use a separate closure variable for the config data so it persists across calls.

exercises.title: Observer Pattern
exercises.description: Create a function called `createEventEmitter` that returns an event emitter object. The emitter has these methods: `on(event, callback)` registers a callback for the named event (the same callback should not be registered twice for the same event); `off(event, callback)` removes a specific callback from the event; `emit(event, ...args)` calls all registered callbacks for the event, passing the extra arguments to each one; `listenerCount(event)` returns the number of callbacks registered for the event (0 if no listeners). Callbacks should fire in the order they were registered.
exercises.hint1: Store listeners as an object where each key is an event name and each value is an array of callback functions. For `on`, push the callback into the array for that event. For `emit`, loop through the array and call each callback with the provided arguments. For `off`, filter out the matching callback.
exercises.hint2: Use `var listeners = {}`. For `on`, create the array if it does not exist, then check `indexOf` before pushing to prevent duplicates. For `emit`, use `Array.prototype.slice.call(arguments, 1)` to capture extra arguments, then use `forEach` to call each callback with `apply`. For `off`, use `filter` to remove the matching callback reference.
exercises.instructions: Create a function called `createEventEmitter` that returns an event emitter object. The emitter has these methods: `on(event, callback)` registers a callback for the named event (the same callback should not be registered twice for the same event); `off(event, callback)` removes a specific callback from the event; `emit(event, ...args)` calls all registered callbacks for the event, passing the extra arguments to each one; `listenerCount(event)` returns the number of callbacks registered for the event (0 if no listeners). Callbacks should fire in the order they were registered.
hints: The observer pattern lets objects subscribe to events and be notified when those events occur. It decouples the event source from the listeners. Each event name maps to a list of callback functions that fire when the event is emitted.
Store listeners in an object keyed by event name, each mapping to an array of callbacks. Prevent duplicate registrations of the same function reference.

exercises.title: Strategy Pattern
exercises.description: Create a `Validator` class that accepts a validation strategy and validates data using it. The constructor takes a strategy object that must have a `validate(data)` method. The `Validator` has these methods: `setStrategy(strategy)` changes the current strategy; `validate(data)` delegates to the current strategy's `validate` method and returns its result; `validateBatch(items)` validates an array of items and returns `{ valid: [...], invalid: [...] }` where each entry is `{ item, result }` (result is whatever the strategy returns). Also create three strategy objects: `emailStrategy` with a `validate(str)` method that returns `{ valid: true/false, message: "..." }` (valid if the string contains `@` and `.` after the `@`); `numberRangeStrategy` with a `validate(obj)` method where `obj` has `value`, `min`, `max` and returns valid if value is within range; `passwordStrategy` with a `validate(str)` method that returns valid if the string is at least 8 characters and contains both a letter and a digit.
exercises.hint1: The Validator class stores a strategy object and delegates all validation to it. Each strategy is a plain object with a `validate` method that returns `{ valid: boolean, message: string }`. The Validator does not need to know how validation works — it just calls the strategy's method. This makes it easy to swap behaviors at runtime.
exercises.hint2: Store `this.strategy` in the constructor. `validate(data)` simply returns `this.strategy.validate(data)`. `setStrategy(s)` replaces `this.strategy`. For `validateBatch`, loop through items, call validate on each, and sort results into `valid` and `invalid` arrays based on the `valid` property of the result.
exercises.instructions: Create a `Validator` class that accepts a validation strategy and validates data using it. The constructor takes a strategy object that must have a `validate(data)` method. The `Validator` has these methods: `setStrategy(strategy)` changes the current strategy; `validate(data)` delegates to the current strategy's `validate` method and returns its result; `validateBatch(items)` validates an array of items and returns `{ valid: [...], invalid: [...] }` where each entry is `{ item, result }` (result is whatever the strategy returns). Also create three strategy objects: `emailStrategy` with a `validate(str)` method that returns `{ valid: true/false, message: "..." }` (valid if the string contains `@` and `.` after the `@`); `numberRangeStrategy` with a `validate(obj)` method where `obj` has `value`, `min`, `max` and returns valid if value is within range; `passwordStrategy` with a `validate(str)` method that returns valid if the string is at least 8 characters and contains both a letter and a digit.
hints: The strategy pattern separates validation logic into interchangeable objects, each with a common interface. The validator delegates to whatever strategy is currently set, making it easy to swap behavior at runtime without changing the validator itself.
The validator delegates its validate call to the current strategy. For batch validation, iterate and sort results into valid and invalid groups based on each result's status.

exercises.title: Decorator Pattern
exercises.description: Create two decorator functions that wrap other functions with additional behavior without modifying the original. First, create `withLogging(fn)` that returns a new function which calls `fn` with the same arguments and returns its result, but also records each call. The wrapper should have a `calls` property (an array) where each entry is `{ args: [...], result: value }`. Second, create `withMemoization(fn)` that returns a new function which caches results based on the `JSON.stringify` of the arguments. If the same arguments are passed again, return the cached result without calling `fn`. The wrapper should have a `cache` property (a plain object) mapping stringified args to results.
exercises.hint1: A decorator is a function that takes a function and returns a new function that adds behavior around the original call. For logging, call the original function, store the args and result in an array on the wrapper, then return the result. For memoization, check a cache object before calling the original — if the result exists, return it; otherwise call the original, store the result, and return it.
exercises.hint2: For `withLogging`, create a wrapper function. Inside it, convert arguments to an array, call `fn.apply(null, args)`, push `{ args, result }` to `wrapper.calls`, and return the result. Set `wrapper.calls = []` before returning the wrapper. For `withMemoization`, use `JSON.stringify(args)` as the cache key. Check `wrapper.cache.hasOwnProperty(key)` before calling `fn`.
exercises.instructions: Create two decorator functions that wrap other functions with additional behavior without modifying the original. First, create `withLogging(fn)` that returns a new function which calls `fn` with the same arguments and returns its result, but also records each call. The wrapper should have a `calls` property (an array) where each entry is `{ args: [...], result: value }`. Second, create `withMemoization(fn)` that returns a new function which caches results based on the `JSON.stringify` of the arguments. If the same arguments are passed again, return the cached result without calling `fn`. The wrapper should have a `cache` property (a plain object) mapping stringified args to results.
hints: The decorator pattern wraps a function with additional behavior -- logging calls or caching results -- without modifying the original. Each decorator returns a new function that intercepts calls, does extra work, and delegates to the original.

Each decorator creates a wrapper function. The wrapper needs to capture the arguments, call the original function, and perform its extra work (recording the call for logging, or checking/storing in a cache for memoization). Attach the tracking data as a property on the wrapper itself.

exercises.title: Mixin Pattern
exercises.description: Create a function called `applyMixins` that takes a target class and any number of mixin objects, and copies all methods from each mixin onto the target class's prototype. Existing methods on the prototype should not be overwritten. Also create three mixin objects: `timestampMixin` with a `getTimestamp()` method that returns the current millisecond timestamp; `serializeMixin` with a `serialize()` method that returns a JSON string of the instance's own enumerable properties, and a `toObject()` method that returns a shallow copy of the instance's own properties as a plain object; `validationMixin` with a `validate(rules)` method that takes an object where each key is a property name and each value is a validation function — it returns `{ valid: true/false, errors: [...] }` where errors is an array of key names that failed validation.
exercises.hint1: Loop through each mixin argument. For each mixin, iterate over its keys and copy the methods onto the target class's prototype — but only if that key does not already exist on the prototype. This preserves existing methods while adding new behaviors from multiple sources.
exercises.hint2: Use `arguments` to access the variable number of mixins. For each mixin, get its keys with `Object.keys(mixin)` and for each key, check `if (!Target.prototype[key])` before assigning `Target.prototype[key] = mixin[key]`. The mixin methods use `this` to access instance properties, which works because they run in the context of the instance when called.
exercises.instructions: Create a function called `applyMixins` that takes a target class and any number of mixin objects, and copies all methods from each mixin onto the target class's prototype. Existing methods on the prototype should not be overwritten. Also create three mixin objects: `timestampMixin` with a `getTimestamp()` method that returns the current millisecond timestamp; `serializeMixin` with a `serialize()` method that returns a JSON string of the instance's own enumerable properties, and a `toObject()` method that returns a shallow copy of the instance's own properties as a plain object; `validationMixin` with a `validate(rules)` method that takes an object where each key is a property name and each value is a validation function — it returns `{ valid: true/false, errors: [...] }` where errors is an array of key names that failed validation.
hints: The mixin pattern copies methods from plain objects onto a class's prototype, giving instances new capabilities without using inheritance. The key rule is that existing prototype methods should not be overwritten -- check before copying each method.
Iterate each mixin's keys and copy them to the target prototype, skipping any key that already exists. Mixin methods use the instance context when called.

exercises.title: Router with Path Parameters
exercises.description: Create a function called `createRouter` that returns a router object. The router has these methods: `addRoute(method, pattern, handler)` registers a handler for a given HTTP method and URL pattern — patterns can include named parameters prefixed with `:` (e.g., `"/users/:id"`); `dispatch(method, path)` finds the matching route and calls its handler with an object of extracted parameters, returning the handler's result. If no route matches, return `{ status: 404, body: "Not Found" }`. Routes must match the HTTP method exactly (case-insensitive) and the path segments. For example, the pattern `"/users/:id/posts/:postId"` should match the path `"/users/42/posts/7"` and extract `{ id: "42", postId: "7" }`.
exercises.hint1: Store registered routes as objects with method, pattern segments, and handler. When dispatching, split the incoming path into segments and compare against each route — static segments must match exactly, and segments starting with `:` are parameters whose values get extracted into an object.
exercises.hint2: For `addRoute`, split the pattern on `/` and store the parts array. For `dispatch`, split the path and loop through routes. For each route, check method match and segment count match, then compare each segment: if the route part starts with `:`, store the path value in a params object using the part name (minus the `:`). If all segments match, call `handler(params)`. If no route matches, return `{ status: 404, body: "Not Found" }`.
exercises.instructions: Create a function called `createRouter` that returns a router object. The router has these methods: `addRoute(method, pattern, handler)` registers a handler for a given HTTP method and URL pattern — patterns can include named parameters prefixed with `:` (e.g., `"/users/:id"`); `dispatch(method, path)` finds the matching route and calls its handler with an object of extracted parameters, returning the handler's result. If no route matches, return `{ status: 404, body: "Not Found" }`. Routes must match the HTTP method exactly (case-insensitive) and the path segments. For example, the pattern `"/users/:id/posts/:postId"` should match the path `"/users/42/posts/7"` and extract `{ id: "42", postId: "7" }`.
hints: A router matches URL paths by splitting them into segments and comparing each one. Path parameters (segments prefixed with a colon) act as wildcards that capture the corresponding value from the actual URL into a params object.

Split both the registered pattern and the incoming path into segments. Match segment by segment -- static segments must match exactly, parameter segments capture their value. Check segment count equality first. Compare HTTP methods case-insensitively.

exercises.title: Middleware Pipeline
exercises.description: Create a function called `createMiddlewarePipeline` that returns a pipeline object. The pipeline has these methods: `use(middlewareFn)` adds a middleware function to the pipeline; `execute(context)` runs all middleware in order and returns the final context. Each middleware function receives `(context, next)` — it can modify the context object and must call `next()` to pass control to the next middleware. If a middleware does not call `next()`, the pipeline stops and returns the context at that point. If any middleware throws an error, the pipeline should catch it and set `context.error` to the error message, then stop execution. The context starts as whatever object is passed to `execute` and accumulates modifications from each middleware.
exercises.hint1: Store middleware functions in an array. When executing, define a `next` function that advances an index counter and calls the current middleware with the context and itself as the `next` argument. Each middleware decides whether to call `next()` to continue the chain.
exercises.hint2: Keep an `index` variable. Define `function next() { if (index < middlewares.length) { var fn = middlewares[index]; index++; fn(context, next); } }`. Wrap the middleware call in try/catch — on error, set `context.error` and stop. Call `next()` once to start the chain. Return the context after the chain completes.
exercises.instructions: Create a function called `createMiddlewarePipeline` that returns a pipeline object. The pipeline has these methods: `use(middlewareFn)` adds a middleware function to the pipeline; `execute(context)` runs all middleware in order and returns the final context. Each middleware function receives `(context, next)` — it can modify the context object and must call `next()` to pass control to the next middleware. If a middleware does not call `next()`, the pipeline stops and returns the context at that point. If any middleware throws an error, the pipeline should catch it and set `context.error` to the error message, then stop execution. The context starts as whatever object is passed to `execute` and accumulates modifications from each middleware.
hints: A middleware pipeline chains functions together using a `next` callback. Each middleware receives a shared context object and decides whether to pass control onward by calling `next()`. If it does not call `next()`, the chain stops. Think of it like a series of gates.
Build a recursive next function that advances through the middleware array. Wrap each invocation in error handling to catch and record failures.

exercises.title: REST API Simulation
exercises.description: Create a function called `createAPI` that returns a simulated REST API for managing a collection of items. Each item has an auto-incremented `id`. The API object has these methods: `get(id)` returns `{ status: 200, body: item }` if found, or `{ status: 404, body: "Not Found" }` if not; `getAll()` returns `{ status: 200, body: [items] }`; `post(data)` validates that `data` has a `name` property (non-empty string), creates an item with an auto-incremented `id`, and returns `{ status: 201, body: newItem }` — or `{ status: 400, body: "Validation Error" }` if invalid; `put(id, data)` updates an existing item and returns `{ status: 200, body: updatedItem }`, or 404 if not found, or 400 if data is invalid; `delete(id)` removes an item and returns `{ status: 200, body: "Deleted" }`, or 404 if not found.
exercises.hint1: Store items in a private array and use a counter for auto-incrementing IDs. Each CRUD method simulates an HTTP response by returning `{ status, body }`. The `post` and `put` methods should validate input before making changes, while `get`, `put`, and `delete` should check if the item exists and return 404 if not.
exercises.hint2: Use `var items = []` and `var nextId = 1`. For `post`, validate `data.name` is a non-empty string, create `{ id: nextId++, name: data.name }`, push to array, return `{ status: 201, body: item }`. For `get`, loop through items to find matching id. For `put`, find the item and update its name. For `delete`, find and splice the item out.
exercises.instructions: Create a function called `createAPI` that returns a simulated REST API for managing a collection of items. Each item has an auto-incremented `id`. The API object has these methods: `get(id)` returns `{ status: 200, body: item }` if found, or `{ status: 404, body: "Not Found" }` if not; `getAll()` returns `{ status: 200, body: [items] }`; `post(data)` validates that `data` has a `name` property (non-empty string), creates an item with an auto-incremented `id`, and returns `{ status: 201, body: newItem }` — or `{ status: 400, body: "Validation Error" }` if invalid; `put(id, data)` updates an existing item and returns `{ status: 200, body: updatedItem }`, or 404 if not found, or 400 if data is invalid; `delete(id)` removes an item and returns `{ status: 200, body: "Deleted" }`, or 404 if not found.
hints: A REST API simulation manages an in-memory collection with CRUD operations. Each method returns a response object with a status code and body, following HTTP conventions. Validation should happen before any data is modified.

Use a private array for storage and a counter for auto-incrementing IDs. Each CRUD method needs to handle the success case and the appropriate error cases (not found, validation failure) with the correct status codes. Think about which operations need to find an item by ID.

exercises.title: In-Memory Database
exercises.description: Create a function called `createDatabase` that takes a schema object and returns a database instance. The schema defines field names and their types (e.g., `{ name: "string", age: "number", active: "boolean" }`). The database has these methods: `insert(record)` validates the record against the schema, assigns an auto-incremented `_id`, and stores it — returns the stored record or throws an error with message `"Validation failed"` if any field has the wrong type or required fields are missing; `findById(id)` returns the record or `null`; `find(query)` returns an array of all records matching every key-value pair in the query object (e.g., `find({ active: true })` returns all active records); `update(id, changes)` merges changes into an existing record (validating changed fields against schema) and returns the updated record or `null` if not found; `remove(id)` deletes a record and returns `true` if found, `false` otherwise; `count()` returns the total number of records.
exercises.hint1: Store records in an array and the schema as a reference for validation. For `insert`, check that every schema field exists in the record and matches the expected `typeof`. For `find`, filter records where every key-value pair in the query matches the record. Use a counter for auto-incrementing `_id` values.
exercises.hint2: For validation, loop through `Object.keys(schema)` and check `typeof record[key] === schema[key]` for each field. For `find(query)`, use `records.filter` where every query key matches the record value. For `update`, validate only the changed fields against the schema, then merge them into the found record. Throw `new Error("Validation failed")` for schema violations.
exercises.instructions: Create a function called `createDatabase` that takes a schema object and returns a database instance. The schema defines field names and their types (e.g., `{ name: "string", age: "number", active: "boolean" }`). The database has these methods: `insert(record)` validates the record against the schema, assigns an auto-incremented `_id`, and stores it — returns the stored record or throws an error with message `"Validation failed"` if any field has the wrong type or required fields are missing; `findById(id)` returns the record or `null`; `find(query)` returns an array of all records matching every key-value pair in the query object (e.g., `find({ active: true })` returns all active records); `update(id, changes)` merges changes into an existing record (validating changed fields against schema) and returns the updated record or `null` if not found; `remove(id)` deletes a record and returns `true` if found, `false` otherwise; `count()` returns the total number of records.
hints: An in-memory database validates records against a schema that maps field names to expected types. The `find` method filters records by checking that every key-value pair in the query matches. Think about how full validation differs from partial validation for updates.
Use typeof checks against the schema for validation. Full validation checks all fields on insert; partial validation checks only changed fields on update.

exercises.title: Application: Expression Evaluator
exercises.description: Create a function called `evaluate` that takes a string containing a mathematical expression with `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, and parentheses, and returns the numeric result. The function must respect standard operator precedence: parentheses first, then `*` and `/` (left to right), then `+` and `-` (left to right). The expression will contain non-negative integers and may have spaces. Examples: `"3 + 4 * 2"` returns `11`, `"(3 + 4) * 2"` returns `14`, `"10 / 2 + 3"` returns `8`. You may assume the input is always a valid expression.
exercises.hint1: Use recursive descent parsing with three levels of precedence: expressions handle `+` and `-`, terms handle `*` and `/`, and factors handle numbers and parenthesized sub-expressions. Tokenize the string first, then walk through the tokens with a position pointer.
exercises.hint2: Tokenize with a regex like `/\d+|[+\-*/()]/g`. Write three functions: `parseExpr` calls `parseTerm` and loops on `+`/`-`; `parseTerm` calls `parseFactor` and loops on `*`/`/`; `parseFactor` handles numbers (return the value) and `(` (recurse into `parseExpr`, then skip `)`). Use a shared position variable that advances as tokens are consumed.
exercises.instructions: Create a function called `evaluate` that takes a string containing a mathematical expression with `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, and parentheses, and returns the numeric result. The function must respect standard operator precedence: parentheses first, then `*` and `/` (left to right), then `+` and `-` (left to right). The expression will contain non-negative integers and may have spaces. Examples: `"3 + 4 * 2"` returns `11`, `"(3 + 4) * 2"` returns `14`, `"10 / 2 + 3"` returns `8`. You may assume the input is always a valid expression.
hints: Evaluating a math expression with correct operator precedence requires separate handling for each precedence level. Addition/subtraction is lowest, multiplication/division is next, and parentheses/numbers are highest. A recursive approach where each level calls the next-higher level works well.

First tokenize the expression string into numbers and operators. Then write functions for each precedence level where each one calls the next-higher level for its operands. The lowest-precedence function handles `+` and `-`, the next handles `*` and `/`, and the highest handles numbers and parenthesized sub-expressions.

exercises.title: Application: Reactive Store
